title: TASKING Extends Toolchain Support to Infineon’s RISC-V AURIX RC1 MCUs - EE Times Asia
content:
Home » EDA » TASKING Extends Toolchain Support to Infineon’s RISC-V AURIX RC1 MCUs TASKING's latest tools will support development and safety qualification of Infineon's next-generation automotive MCUs. TASKING has extended its embedded software development tools to support Infineon Technologies’ AURIX RC1 family of RISC-V-based automotive microcontrollers, covering compilation, debugging and software verification. The toolchain combines TASKING’s VX-toolset compiler, winIDEA debugging environment and BlueBox hardware debugging platform with LDRA verification tools. It also incorporates agentic AI capabilities intended to reduce development effort for complex multicore automotive systems. Unveiled by Infineon at electronica 2026, AURIX RC1 uses a RISC-V-based multicore real-time cluster architecture targeting software-defined vehicles (SDVs), software-defined everything (SDX) and Physical AI applications. The family is designed to address requirements for real-time processing, functional safety, security and edge AI. 【Free Download】Delivering Best-in-Class Precision Analog with the Treo Platform The unified toolchain is intended to ease migration from Infineon’s TriCore architecture and Arm-based platforms. Developers moving from TriCore can retain existing development tools, CI/CD pipelines and workflows, while Arm users can work across Arm and RISC-V platforms within the same environment. “We consider the introduction of our new AURIX RC1 family much beyond the new microcontroller architecture itself,” said Thomas Schneid, Vice President Software and Ecosystem Management at Infineon. “Our new open architecture based on RISC-V comes with a growing holistic ecosystem. Together with partners like TASKING, we are creating an open and scalable software, tools and services environment that enables customers to build on their existing investments, simplify migration and accelerate innovation on AURIX RC1.” The integrated development environment is designed to support software development against ISO 26262 functional safety and ISO/SAE 21434 cybersecurity requirements. Support for AURIX RC1 virtual prototypes also allows developers to begin software evaluation, testing and verification before physical silicon becomes available. TASKING is adding agentic AI functions to its compiler and debugging tools. AI skills for the VX-toolset, scheduled for release in December 2026, will provide compiler-related assistance through a Visual Studio Code environment using the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Functions include build diagnostics, map-file and LSL analysis, and startup-code support. The winIDEA AI Kit is also intended to automate parts of debugging. TASKING reported at least 50% effort reduction in three use cases, although it did not provide further details on the measurements. The company said engineers retain control over critical operations, with human approval required for consequential actions. One application is worst-case execution time (WCET) analysis for functional safety. AI assistance can help generate test scripts, compile software with different configurations and evaluate task combinations to identify multicore timing interactions that could affect deterministic operation. “As a trusted partner with Infineon for more than 40 years, TASKING has worked directly with Infineon to design tools for AURIX from the inside out,” said Christoph Herzog, Co-CEO & CTO, TASKING. “OEMs can be confident their toolchain is optimized for the silicon, aligned with Infineon’s software ecosystem, and designed to accelerate and simplify even the most complex automotive designs. In addition, our guiding principle, ‘AI assists, engineers decide,’ enables us to support Agentic AI across the toolchain while maintaining functional safety and simplifying certification.” TASKING’s collaboration with Infineon dates back more than four decades, covering development tools for the C166 and TriCore architectures. The company has also participated in five Infineon DRIVECORE software bundles and worked with Infineon on its RISC-V software development kit and virtual prototypes. The RISC-V VX-toolset supporting AURIX RC1 is scheduled to become available in December 2026, with toolchain qualification planned for 2027. Infineon also plans to include TASKING compiler technology in its DRIVECORE software portfolio for the new MCU family, providing developers with a pre-integrated combination of software and development tools. title: Midlakes vs East score, updates from Section V boys volleyball title game - Democrat and Chronicle
content: CANANDAIGUA – Midlakes proved that records need not matter once postseason play begins. Midlakes, the three-time defending Section V Class B2 champion, entered the 2026 sectional playoffs with a record of 9-10. The Screaming Eagles didn’t just move above .500 – they extended their reign over Class B2. What’s better than three consecutive Section V boys volleyball championships? Four, of course. No. 4 Midlakes (12-10) defeated No. 3 East High (13-6) in straight sets (28-26, 25-18, 25-16) to win another Class B2 title Nov. 10 at Finger Lakes Community College. Jesse Bennett won Most Valuable Player of the Class B2 tournament, joining teammates Joah Bennett and Walker Landschoot on the all-tournament team. This victory occurred after Midlakes knocked off top-seeded North Rose-Wolcott in the Class B2 semifinals. It will now play the Class B1 champion for the right to represent Section V in state tournament play. Look back at how the Class B2 final unfolded below. Midlakes won the third set, 25-16, to complete a sweep of East High and win its fourth consecutive Section V Class B2 boys volleyball championship. Walker Landschoot finished it with a kill for the Screaming Eagles. They finished the match on a 14-5 run. Colt Walker, Austin Teed and Dominic Karl's attacking at the net helped Midlakes built its third-set lead. Evan Everson enjoyed a late run at the service line, as well. Midlakes and East split the first 22 points scored in set three. Timeout called on the floor as the teams trade blows tied, 11-11. Evan Everson sealed a 25-18 win for Midlakes in the second set with an ace on set point. Midlakes led the whole way, albeit narrowly, largely thanks to the attacking of Jesse Bennett. Duke VanSavage, as he did in the first set, moved the Screaming Eagles within set point with a kill. Midlakes now leads, 2-0, and is one set victory away from repeating again as Class B2 champion. Jesse and Joah Bennett, two of Midlakes' top attackers, appear to have settled in against East. Thunderous kills by the Bennetts have helped Midlakes maintain a small lead throughout the second set. Timeout called by East with Midlakes leading, 15-11. Midlakes prevailed to win the first set, 28-26, on an ace by Jesse Bennett. Duke VanSavage gave the Screaming Eagles a 27-26 lead on a kill which fell just inside the out-of-bounds line near East's bench. East enjoyed a 24-23 lead when a kill by Joah Bennett kept Midlakes alive. A hit out-of-bounds by East then extended the set after a Midlakes service error. Walker Landschoot's ace gave Midlakes set point at 26-25, but Yandiel Tolentino-Lopez answered with a kill for East. Then came VanSavage and Jesse Bennett's decisive attacks. Midlakes enjoyed a 6-0 scoring run after its timeout. East, however, counter-punched with an 9-2 run which left it with a 20-15 lead in the first set. Jadiel Santiago has stepped up at the net for East, which remains on the attack while Midlakes tries to block. Midlakes called the first timeout of the match after falling behind East, 9-7, in the first set. Yandiel Tolentino-Lopez and John Hart IV led the Eagles' early offense. They've traded serves with Midlkaes thus far. Midlakes and East are scheduled for a 6 p.m. start on Nov. 10. Finger Lakes Community College's Putt Moore Gymnasium, located at 3325 Marvin Sands Dr in Canandaigua, will host the Section V Class B2 boys volleyball final.

title: Girls night, Italian food and disco balls: A night at V Modern Italian - That's So Tampa
content:
If you’re looking for your next girls’ night out in Tampa, the brand-new V Modern Italian in North Hyde Park needs to be on your radar. The new Italian hotspot, located at 1701 W North A St in North Hyde Park, officially celebrates its grand opening this week following its recent soft opening. I recently spent an evening here with my girlfriends, and it was so much more than dinner. Think Wynwood, Miami vibes with colorful murals, incredible artwork, moody lighting, and a stunning bar. As the night goes on, dinner transitions into nightlife with disco balls, a DJ, and an atmosphere that makes you want to stay all night. ADVERTISEMENT


Discover moreTampa travel guideTampa event ticketsTampa Bay events We came hungry, and the food did not disappoint. We started with the Antipasti Tower, featuring marinara meatballs, focaccia tartufata, and burrata al limoncello, perfect for sharing. If you can’t decide what to order, this is the hack to try a little bit of everything. For our mains, we tried the Black Truffle Pipette with 72-hour short rib and black truffle cream, Manicotti della Casa with ricotta and parmesan cream, On the Bone Lamb Shank with truffle risotto, and Salmone in Crosta with a Mediterranean herb crust. We were impressed by them all. The cocktails were equally impressive, especially the Seafoam Margarita with its citrus air topping, and the Going Coastal, a tropical hibiscus-passionfruit cocktail with a mezcal mist. Even if you aren’t hungry, V Modern is worth trying just to meet up for drinks. We ended the night with the Cannoli Concierge, a fun tableside experience featuring freshly filled cannoli with your choice of pistachio, chocolate espresso, or toffee toppings. The tableside presentation was yet another one of the extra touches that makes the overall experience so memorable and so enjoyable for a group. What I loved most about V Modern Italian was how seamlessly it blends an elevated Italian dinner with a genuinely fun night out. Between the music, lighting, artwork, cocktails, and overall energy, it felt like a little escape to Miami without leaving Tampa. Whether you’re planning a birthday, girls’ night, or just an excuse to dress up and grab cocktails, this new North Hyde Park hotspot is one to add to your list! title: Deductibility of Criminal Defense and Post-Conviction Legal Fees Under Section 162: The Court of Federal Claims Decision in Anderson v. United States - Current Federal Tax Developments
content: A site devoted to articles on current developments in federal taxes geared toward CPAs in tax practice. Anderson v. United States, No. 18-1133T, Fed. Cl,. Nov. 9, 2026 For tax professionals representing individuals and closely held business owners, determining the deductibility of legal expenses under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 162(a) requires a rigorous application of the “origin of the claim” doctrine. On November 9, 2026, the United States Court of Federal Claims issued a published opinion in Anderson v. United States that offers critical guidance on the intersection of trade or business deductions, collateral estoppel across successive tax years, and the jurisdictional limits of tax refund tribunals when confronted with collateral attacks on underlying criminal convictions. Writing for the court, Judge Stephen S. Schwartz granted summary judgment in favor of the government, holding that the taxpayers were collaterally estopped from relitigating the business characterization of post-conviction legal fees and reaffirming that a civil tax forum lacks subject-matter jurisdiction to re-examine or disregard a final state court criminal conviction. Plaintiff William French Anderson is a physician, pediatric specialist, and geneticist. His wife and co-plaintiff, Kathryn D. Anderson, is also a physician; however, because the underlying operative facts did not concern her directly, the court focused its inquiry on Dr. Anderson. In 2006, a California state jury convicted Dr. Anderson of sexually abusing a minor—specifically, the daughter of a colleague employed at his laboratory—while providing the minor with karate instruction and academic tutoring at his private residence (People v. Anderson, 144 Cal. Rptr. 3d 606, 609 (Cal. Ct. App. 2012)). The judgment of conviction was affirmed on direct appeal (id. at 640). Over the subsequent two decades, Dr. Anderson engaged in extensive, unsuccessful post-conviction litigation across state and federal courts (see, e.g., In re Anderson, No. B232746, 2013 WL 4759680 (Cal. Ct. App. Sept. 5, 2013); Anderson v. Perez, No. CV 14-09463, 2016 WL 8078147 (C.D. Cal. Nov. 8, 2016), report and recommendation adopted, 2017 WL 379400 (C.D. Cal. Jan. 24, 2017)). A petition claiming actual innocence was also filed in California state court (People v. Anderson, No. BA255257 (Cal. Super. Ct. L.A. Cnty. Jan. 29, 2024)). Central to Dr. Anderson’s defense and post-conviction strategy was his contention that he was “the victim of an elaborate scheme by the Chinese government to frame him and steal his intellectual property concerning a cancer drug he was developing.” He asserted that the evidence against him was falsified as part of an institutional espionage and sabotage campaign orchestrated by his former laboratory colleague. The taxpayers initiated two separate judicial proceedings to establish that Dr. Anderson’s post-conviction legal expenses were deductible under IRC § 162(a). The first proceeding arose in the United States Tax Court regarding deficiency assessments for tax years 2013 and 2014 (Anderson v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-42, 2023 WL 2660324 (Mar. 28, 2023), aff’d, No. 23-9002, 2024 WL 2239160 (10th Cir. May 17, 2024)). In that litigation, the taxpayers argued that evidence uncovered in 2013 and 2014 established that the criminal charges were designed to sabotage Dr. Anderson’s medical research business, meaning that his legal fees stemmed directly from his trade or business. The Tax Court rejected this position, ruling that the underlying conduct was personal, though it allowed a narrow $13,000 business deduction for fees paid to an independent IT consultant who performed investigatory work into corporate sabotage. The second proceeding—the subject of the present Court of Federal Claims opinion—concerned tax years 2011 and 2012. For these earlier years, the taxpayers timely filed joint returns, paid their assessed income taxes, and subsequently filed administrative refund claims with the Internal Revenue Service. On their amended returns, the taxpayers asserted that “the taxpayer has incurred and deducted legal fees associated with criminal charges originating from his trade or business,” seeking refunds based on legal fees paid to habeas defense counsel Douglas W. Otto. Following the IRS’s formal disallowance of their refund claims, the taxpayers filed a refund complaint in the Court of Federal Claims pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(1). Under IRC § 162(a), taxpayers may deduct “ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business.” To qualify, an expenditure must be “appropriate and helpful to the taxpayer’s business and that results from an activity which is a common and accepted practice” (Amdahl Corp. v. Commissioner, 108 T.C. 507, 523 (1997)). Furthermore, the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of clearly establishing statutory entitlement to the deduction claimed (Principal Life Insurance Co. & Subsidiaries v. United States, 116 Fed. Cl. 82, 100 (2014), quoting Interstate Transit Lines v. Commissioner, 319 U.S. 590, 593 (1943)). In determining whether litigation expenses—civil or criminal—qualify as deductible trade or business expenses under § 162, federal courts apply the long-standing “origin and character of the claim” standard established by the Supreme Court in United States v. Gilmore, 372 U.S. 39, 49 (1963). As reiterated by the Federal Circuit, the deductibility of legal fees depends not on the potential financial or reputational consequences to the taxpayer’s enterprise, but exclusively on the “origin and character of the claim underlying the expense incurred” (Dana Corp. v. United States, 174 F.3d 1344, 1350 (Fed. Cir. 1999)). Historically, where criminal charges originate directly from profit-seeking business activities, legal expenses incurred in defending against those charges are deductible (Commissioner v. Tellier, 383 U.S. 687, 690–93 (1966); Silberman v. United States, 40 Fed. Cl. 895, 906 (1998)). Conversely, where the underlying conduct is personal, the expenses remain nondeductible personal expenses under IRC § 262, regardless of the devastating collateral impact a conviction may have on the taxpayer’s professional license, business reputation, or ongoing livelihood (see, e.g., Siket v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1978-124 (denying deduction to police officer defending against off-duty assault charges); Argyle v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-218 (disallowing CPA’s defense costs for off-premises, non-business personal conduct); Swift v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-13). The threshold defense raised by the Department of Justice was collateral estoppel (issue preclusion). In the Federal Circuit, collateral estoppel bars relitigation when: “(1) the issue to be decided is identical to one decided in the first action; (2) the issue was actually litigated in the first action; (3) resolution of the issue was essential to a final judgment in the first action; and (4) the parties had a full and fair opportunity to litigate the issue in the first action” (Arkla, Inc. v. United States, 37 F.3d 621, 624 (Fed. Cir. 1994), citing Mother’s Restaurant, Inc. v. Mama’s Pizza, Inc., 723 F.2d 1566, 1569 (Fed. Cir. 1983)). In the specialized context of federal taxation involving successive tax years, identicality of issues is governed by the “separability” doctrine articulated in Commissioner v. Sunnen, 333 U.S. 591, 601 (1948). Under Sunnen, tax years are separable only in two limited situations: Applying this standard, Judge Schwartz noted that the taxpayers identified no change in statutory, regulatory, or judicial standards between the 2011–2012 tax years and the 2013–2014 tax years reviewed by the Tax Court. Turning to factual separability, the court emphasized: “The only evident difference is the tax years alone, which is not enough by itself to establish separability.” The court pointed out that the Tax Court had made an explicit factual determination that Dr. Anderson’s criminal conduct was personal and unrelated to his trade or business. As Judge Schwartz observed: “That is a finding about historical facts that predate the tax years at issue: Whether Dr. Anderson is innocent or guilty as a factual matter, the nature of his charged conduct must be the same for all subsequent tax years. On that issue, there is no way to establish a difference between the tax years, as the separability test requires.” Furthermore, the taxpayers failed to establish any variance in the actual nature of the legal work performed by defense counsel Mr. Otto. For 2013 and 2014, the Tax Court found “no evidence” that payments to Mr. Otto were incurred to investigate trade secret theft rather than to pursue standard state habeas relief (Anderson v. Commissioner, 2024 WL 2239160, at *4). Because Mr. Otto’s billing descriptions and the underlying character of his work were identical across 2011 and 2012, the taxpayers were bound by the prior adverse factual determination. The court also identified an insurmountable temporal contradiction in the taxpayers’ position. In the Tax Court, the taxpayers maintained that their investigation into IP espionage arose from “new evidence discovered in 2013 and 2014.” Addressing this chronological flaw, Judge Schwartz wrote: “Plaintiffs could not have spent money in 2011 or 2012 to investigate evidence that they did not discover until at least the following tax year. So if Plaintiffs’ legal expenses in 2013 and 2014 were not related to the investigation, their expenses in 2011 and 2012 must not have been either.” Finally, while the Tax Court had allowed a limited $13,000 deduction for an IT consultant’s corporate investigation fees in 2013–2014, the taxpayers failed to identify or allocate any specific consultant payments for 2011–2012, resulting in forfeiture of that argument (DecisionPoint Corp. v. United States, 174 Fed. Cl. 475, 482 n.2 (2024)). Seeking to bypass the preclusive bar of collateral estoppel, the taxpayers invoked the “special circumstances” exception recognized in Montana v. United States, 440 U.S. at 155, arguing that newly discovered evidence establishing Dr. Anderson’s actual innocence justified relitigating the origin of the legal fees. Judge Schwartz firmly rejected this theory, highlighting both doctrinal and jurisdictional impediments. Under the Gilmore framework: “The ‘origin and character’ of a claim presumably does not depend on whether the claim is true or false — only on its nature.” Citing Duntley v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1987-579, the court underscored that neither the lack of merit nor the allegedly fabricated nature of an underlying lawsuit transforms its inherent character. The purpose of a legal expenditure is fixed when the liability is incurred and cannot be altered retroactively by subsequent evidentiary revelations. More fundamentally, the Court of Federal Claims addressed the constitutional and statutory limitations on its subject-matter jurisdiction. Under Tucker Act jurisprudence, the Court of Federal Claims possesses no jurisdiction over criminal proceedings (Kurt v. United States, 103 Fed. Cl. 384, 388 (2012), citing Joshua v. United States, 17 F.3d 378, 379–80 (Fed. Cir. 1994)), lacks authority to review or vacate criminal convictions (Reed v. United States, 25 Fed. App’x 903, 904 (Fed. Cir. 2001)), and cannot function as an appellate tribunal over state or federal court judgments (Double Lion Uchet Express Trust v. United States, 149 Fed. Cl. 415, 420 (2020)). Because Dr. Anderson’s state court conviction remains undisturbed on the docket, the court was legally prohibited from entertaining claims that the underlying offenses were a fabrication. In unambiguous terms, Judge Schwartz held: “For all intents and purposes, this Court must assume that Dr. Anderson is guilty — regardless of Plaintiffs’ claims to the contrary.” The court delineated the strict boundary governing tax refund inquiries: “This Court may look to the nature of charged conduct and decide whether it is connected to the taxpayer’s business. What it may not do is decide or assume, after conviction, that the charged conduct did not take place.” Given that the charged and convicted offenses—sexual abuse of a minor during tutoring and karate lessons at the taxpayer’s residence—were undeniably personal, the court concluded that “it is hard to imagine how his legal expenses could have had the required nexus to his medical practice or research.” The Court of Federal Claims granted summary judgment to the United States and dismissed the taxpayers’ complaint with prejudice, establishing two controlling legal conclusions: First, collateral estoppel precludes taxpayers from relitigating the business nature of legal expenses under IRC § 162 in a subsequent refund action when the identical characterization was fully litigated and decided against them for other tax years, absent a demonstrable change in controlling law or material historical facts. Mere difference in calendar tax years does not satisfy the Sunnen separability test. Second, in applying the Gilmore origin-of-the-claim doctrine to criminal defense expenditures, federal tax tribunals must accept the legal validity and finality of underlying criminal convictions. A taxpayer cannot convert personal defense costs into deductible business expenses by collaterally asserting actual innocence or claiming that criminal charges originated from an external conspiracy against their business. title: Confirmed! The Reborn Lotus Esprit Supercar Will Breathe Fire Through a 670-HP V-8 - Car and Driver
content: The twin-turbo 4.0-liter engine will pair with a hybrid system, and the duo will make nearly 1000 horsepower combined. There’s a new V-8-powered Lotus on the way, and we’ve just got our first proper look at the powertrain. While the supercar uses the codename Type 135, most of the world expects it to resurrect the British brand’s legendary Espirt nameplate, and now we know that it’ll have a brand-new 4.0-liter V-8. The engine will team up with a dual-clutch automatic transmission, and both will be built by a company called Horse Powertrain. The twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V-8, called the Horse W40, will come in a hot-V configuration, meaning it’ll store its turbos between the cylinder banks, rather than on either side of them. Horse says the combustion half of the powertrain will be responsible for generating 670 horsepower and 590 pound-feet of torque, though it’ll be part of a larger hybrid system that Lotus promises will combine for at least 986 horsepower. With the engine weighing just 441 pounds, that’s quite a power-dense mill. Rather than pair it with another company’s transmission, Horse built its own eight-speed dual-clutch automatic called the Horse 8LDCT. The gearbox features a sports car-grade wet dual clutch, which is claimed to enable sub-20-millisecond shift responses, along with a silicon-carbide control system and a variable-displacement mechanical pump. Horse’s new powertrain components will make their debut on what’s expected to be the upcoming Lotus Esprit. Unfortunately, the car’s production is still some time away, with Lotus planning to reveal and launch the model in 2028. title: Benda Enters The Adventure Segment With New Capra 700 V-Twin - ADV Pulse
content:
Chinese motorcycle manufacturer Benda has taken its boldest step yet beyond its cruiser roots with the unveiling of the new Capra 700 at EICMA 2026. Developed intentionally for the European market, the middleweight adventure bike marks the company’s first entry into the ADV segment and introduces a platform that blends distinctive styling with a surprisingly capable chassis package. Over the last decade, Benda has built its reputation on unconventional motorcycles that prioritize strong visual identity and engineering originality. Cruiser models like the LFC700 with its massive rear tire and the V4-powered Dark Flag have helped the brand stand out in a crowded marketplace. The Capra 700 continues that design-led approach while targeting one of motorcycling’s most competitive categories. Developed with input from Benda’s European design team in Austria and engineers in Hangzhou, China, the Capra takes its name from the Latin genus of the ibex, a mountain goat known for its agility on challenging terrain. The bike’s styling reflects that inspiration, with compact proportions, a high-mounted front fender, integrated crash bars, distinctive daytime running lights, and exposed mechanical elements giving it a rugged appearance. What makes the Capra particularly interesting, however, is that it appears to offer considerably more than just eye-catching design. Power comes from a new 691.6cc liquid-cooled 65-degree V-twin producing 72.4 horsepower (54 kW) at 9,000 rpm and 50 lb-ft (68 Nm) of torque at 6,500 rpm. While those numbers won’t top the middleweight class, the choice of a V-twin stands out in a segment increasingly dominated by parallel twins. Benda describes the Capra as a road-focused adventure bike, but the chassis specifications suggest a machine capable of venturing well beyond the pavement. The bike rides on a 21-inch front and 18-inch rear wheel combination and features fully-adjustable suspension at both ends, with 9.1 inches (230 mm) of front travel and 8.7 inches (220 mm) at the rear. A steel trellis frame, aluminum swingarm, linkage-equipped rear shock with piggyback reservoir, and switchable electronic rider aids round out the package. Along with its suspension travel and adventure-ready equipment, Benda claims a curb weight of 485 pounds (220 kg) with fluids, placing it in competitive territory with bikes like the Yamaha Tenere 700 World Raid. Additional features worth mentioning include full LED lighting, ride-by-wire throttle, traction control, dual-channel ABS, a slipper clutch, vertical TFT display, USB-A charging port, tank bag mounting slots built into the fuel tank, full wrap-around handguards, skidplate, tubeless spoke wheels, and a rear luggage rack. The Capra brings a distinctive look to a segment where many motorcycles have begun to converge around similar styling themes. Combined with its characterful V-twin engine and off-road oriented chassis, Benda’s first adventure bike could prove to be a legitimate middleweight ADV contender. Benda operates from a European headquarters in Salzburg, Austria, and continues to expand through a growing global distribution network. The company’s motorcycles are already available in Canada through distributor Arcnexus Inc., while Benda lists KEEWAY Group as its distribution partner for the United States. No pricing or market availability details have been announced for the Capra 700, and the company has not confirmed plans to bring the model to North America at this time. title: Latest Federal Court Case: Google LLC v. DDC Tech., LLC - JD Supra
content:
Google LLC v. DDC Tech., LLC, No. 2025-1315 (Fed. Cir. Nov. 5, 2026) In our Case of the Week, the Federal Circuit affirmed three inter partes review decisions holding that Google had failed to establish the obviousness of DDC Tech’s patents covering smartphone-based virtual reality viewers. Among other things, the court rejected Google’s argument that the Board violated the Administrative Procedure Act by unfairly “surprising” Google with an implicit claim construction. The case concerned DDC Tech’s U.S. Patent Nos. 9,420,075; 10,528,199; and 11,093,001 covering smartphone-based virtual reality viewers. Some early smartphone-based VR viewers worked by enclosing a smartphone inside a housing and using optical lenses to create a 3D viewing experience. While this arrangement allowed the smartphone to function as a VR display, it obstructed the user’s access to the touchscreen. The three patents at issue, addressed that problem through an externally accessible input mechanism that could contact the enclosed smartphone’s touchscreen and generate a detectable “touch event.” Google challenged the patents as obvious over two prior art references. The first reference, a patent to “Kondo,” described a smartphone viewer with a remote touch circuit allowing the user to operate the phone from outside the viewer. The second reference, “Chu,” described a mechanical button arrangement for operating a touchscreen inside a waterproof housing. The Board found some, but not all, of the challenged claims unpatentable, and Google appealed the rulings concerning the surviving claims to the Federal Circuit. One issue on appeal concerned the claim construction of a “linkage element” that is “made from flexible material.”  In the proceedings below, Google argued that a spring and a shaft in Chu’s touchscreen mechanism together satisfied that requirement, and that the spring itself was flexible. The Board agreed that the spring was flexible but not that the limitation was present in the prior art, because Google did not show that the shaft itself was made from a flexible material. The Board reasoned that the claim required an entire “linkage element” to be made of flexible materials, as opposed to only part of the element. On appeal, Google challenged that interpretation, and also argued that the Board violated the APA by adopting an allegedly unexpected claim construction in its final written decision. The Federal Circuit disagreed, holding that Board’s position did not amount to an APA violation. The Court distinguished its prior decision in SAS Institute, Inc. v. ComplementSoft, LLC, where the it had held that a change in claim constructions between the Board’s institution decision and its final written decision violated the APA because in that case, neither party could “anticipat[e] that already interpreted terms were actually moving targets, and it [was] thus unreasonable to expect that [the parties] would have briefed or argued, in the alternative, hypothetical constructions not asserted by their opponent.” Here, the Court held that “Google did not face such undue surprise,” because it knew the Board’s position on the relevant claim language “was potentially a moving target.” The Court noted the Board’s institution decision neither construed “linkage element … made from a flexible material” nor accepted Google’s position that the element need not be made exclusively from flexible material. Instead, it expressly invited further argument and evidence on that limitation. However, Google failed to address the claim language further following institution, and on these facts, the Federal Circuit found that “[t]he Board cannot be faulted under the APA for Google’s failure to develop its position.” Accordingly, the Court rejected Google’s APA challenge. Google’s other challenges on appeal were also unsuccessful. Google argued that the Board’s findings on objective indicia of non-obviousness lacked sufficient factual support, but the Court concluded that the record adequately supported those findings. Google also challenged the weight the Board gave that evidence in its overall obviousness analysis. Although the combined prior art disclosed the relevant claim limitations and the Board found a reason to combine the references, however, the Court agreed that the strong copying evidence and moderately weighted industry praise could outweigh Google’s prior-art showing, providing sufficient evidence for the Board’s conclusion that Google had not established obviousness. The Court also rejected Google’s other challenges to the Board’s claim constructions. Accordingly, the Federal Circuit affirmed the Board’s ruling that Google failed to prove certain claims of the ’075, ’199, and ’001 patents unpatentable.  The full opinion can be found here. title: Conservation Easement Valuation and the Fallacy of Hypothetical Mineral Exploitation: Tax Court Rebuffs Discounted Cash Flow in Riddle Aggregates v. Commissioner - Current Federal Tax Developments
content: A site devoted to articles on current developments in federal taxes geared toward CPAs in tax practice. Riddle Aggregates, LLC, Ornstein-Schuler, LLC, Tax Matters Partner v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, T.C. Memo. 2026-117, November 10, 2026 For certified public accountants and enrolled agents advising clients on conservation contributions, partnership taxation, and valuation controversies, the United States Tax Court’s decision in Riddle Aggregates, LLC v. Commissioner provides an instructive dissection of the valuation mechanics governing conservation easements. The opinion forcefully reinforces the judicial consensus regarding the severe limitations of discounted cash flow (DCF) modeling for unmined, undeveloped real property, the preeminence of comparable sales under the principle of substitution, the probative weight of recent arm’s-length entity-level transactions, and the strict, non-waivable application of the 40% gross valuation misstatement penalty under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 6662(h). The case arose from a syndicated conservation easement transaction structured in Morgan County, Alabama, within the Huntsville-Decatur-Albertville Combined Statistical Area. The subject real estate consisted of a 231.22-acre parcel, designated as Tract Two (the Riddle Property), which was carved out of a larger 2,744.30-acre parent tract originally acquired on May 8, 2006, by Freeman Five, LLC (Freeman Five), an entity managed by James Freeman Sr., an experienced real estate trader who had executed over fifty transactions. While portions of the property had historically been used for agriculture and remained fallow as of the valuation date, the property had never been utilized for commercial mining. In early 2017, Freeman Five engaged a land brokerage firm to market the parent tract. At the time, Freeman Five was under no financial distress. Longleaf Ventures, LLC (Longleaf), an entity affiliated with promoters Matthew Ornstein and Frank A. Schuler IV (operating collectively through Ornstein-Schuler, LLC, or OSI), submitted letters of intent in March and April 2017 to acquire approximately 1,451 acres of the parent tract at a contract price of $2,500 per acre. To execute the acquisition and subsequent syndication, the promoters orchestrated a multi-tiered entity structure: Simultaneously, the promoters procured preliminary geotechnical and feasibility studies. Longleaf engaged ECS Southeast LP (ECS) to perform geotechnical exploration. ECS completed two exploratory borings with rock coring, testing one sample from each boring, and issued a report on August 7, 2017, identifying Bangor limestone formation bedrock alongside Pottsville formation sandstone. Riddle subsequently engaged Galt Mining Investments, LLC, which retained Blethen Mine Consultants, LLC (Blethen). Blethen issued reports on October 13 and November 22, 2017, asserting that the parcel contained 25,596,000 tons of proven mineral reserves. Utilizing a 15-year DCF projection discounted at 12%, Blethen modeled a hypothetical limestone quarry on the raw land having a net present value of $45,412,000. Weibel & Associates, Inc. (Weibel) adopted Blethen’s DCF figures to appraise a conservation easement on the parcel at $44,995,000. The promoters then marketed membership units in Riddle Aggregates Group (RAG), the syndication vehicle holding an option to acquire the membership interests in Riddle. RAG issued a Confidential Private Placement Memorandum (PPM) dated October 30, 2017, offering 999 units at $7,397 per unit ($7,397,000 total offering). While the PPM listed four theoretical options—conservation donation, quarry development, holding for appreciation, or leasing to a mine operator—it heavily cautioned investors that mining was “a highly complex, expensive, and potentially dangerous process” that “would probably require significant additional capital.” The PPM specifically warned that “only potential Investors who are not focused on maximizing the potential cash return from an investment in the membership interest in the Company should consider subscribing.” The offering was fully subscribed by 74 investors contributing $7,397,000. On December 5, 2017, RAG acquired a 97.99% interest in Riddle for $6,923,466, with Ornstein-Schuler, LLC (OS LLC) retaining 0.01% and Freeman Five members retaining 2%. On December 8, 2017, Riddle executed a deed conveying a conservation easement encumbering 227.95 acres to Atlantic Coast Conservancy, Inc. Five days later, on December 13, 2017, Riddle donated the underlying fee simple interest in the entire 231.22-acre tract, subject to the easement, to Atlantic Coast Conservancy Properties, LLC. The recorded sales validation form accompanying the fee transfer listed the county tax assessor’s market value at $352,071. On its timely filed Form 1065, U.S. Return of Partnership Income, for the short tax period ending December 31, 2017, Riddle claimed noncash charitable contribution deductions totaling $45,350,000 under IRC Section 170: The return was audited under the unified partnership audit procedures of the Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act of 1982 (TEFRA), IRC Sections 6221 through 6234 (prior to repeal by the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015). On August 23, 2021, the Internal Revenue Service issued a Notice of Final Partnership Administrative Adjustment (FPAA) completely disallowing the $44,995,000 conservation easement deduction, disallowing $10,000 of the fee simple deduction, and asserting accuracy-related penalties under IRC Section 6662, including the 40% gross valuation misstatement penalty under Section 6662(h). Petitioner OS LLC, as Tax Matters Partner, filed a timely petition in the Tax Court. Prior to trial, the parties narrowed the disputed issues through three successive Stipulations of Settled Issues: Consequently, the issues tried before the Tax Court were limited to: (1) the unencumbered fair market value of the Riddle Property before the donation and the resulting value of the conservation easement under Treasury Regulation Section 1.170A-14(h)(3)(i); and (2) whether the partnership was liable for accuracy-related penalties under IRC Section 6662, specifically the 40% gross valuation misstatement penalty under Section 6662(h). As a preliminary matter, petitioner argued that the burden of proof on valuation should shift to the Commissioner pursuant to IRC Section 7491(a)(1) and (2), contending that it had complied with all substantiation and recordkeeping requirements and fully cooperated during the administrative audit. Judge Kerrigan summarily rejected this contention. Citing Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111 (1933), Republic Plaza Properties Partnership v. Commissioner, 107 T.C. 94 (1996), and INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79 (1992), the court noted that IRS adjustments in an FPAA are presumed correct and deductions are a matter of legislative grace. Under IRC Section 7491(a)(1), the burden shifts only if the taxpayer introduces credible evidence, and as established in Knudsen v. Commissioner, 131 T.C. 185 (2008), a burden shift possesses operational significance only in the event of an evidentiary tie. Judge Kerrigan stated: “We have discerned no evidentiary tie on any relevant factual question and are able to decide the issues here on the preponderance of the evidence.” Furthermore, the court observed that pursuant to Dynamo Holdings Ltd. Partnership v. Commissioner, 150 T.C. 224 (2018), the Commissioner does not bear the burden of production for penalties in TEFRA partnership-level proceedings. Under Treasury Regulation Section 1.170A-1(c)(2), fair market value represents “the price at which the property would change hands between a willing buyer and a willing seller, neither being under any compulsion to buy or sell and both having reasonable knowledge of relevant facts.” Because sales of conservation easements are rare and an established market rarely exists (Symington v. Commissioner, 87 T.C. 892 (1986)), courts apply the “before and after” valuation methodology under Treasury Regulation Section 1.170A-14(h)(3)(i). Under this construct, the easement’s value equals the fair market value of the unencumbered property before the grant minus the fair market value of the encumbered property remaining after the donation (TOT Property Holdings, LLC v. Commissioner, 1 F.4th 1354 (11th Cir. 2021)). A critical element of the before-valuation is the determination of the property’s highest and best use (HBU) on the valuation date (Treas. Reg. § 1.170A-14(h)(3)(i), (ii); Stanley Works & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, 87 T.C. 389 (1986)). To qualify as highest and best use, a proposed use must satisfy four foundational criteria: it must be (1) legally permissible, (2) physically possible, (3) financially feasible, and (4) maximally productive (Ranch Springs, LLC v. Commissioner, 164 T.C. 93 (2025); Whitehouse Hotel Ltd. Partnership v. Commissioner, 139 T.C. 304 (2012)). Reviewing Eleventh Circuit precedent, Judge Kerrigan highlighted that strict application of the four traditional factors is not required, as articulated in Savannah Shoals, LLC v. Commissioner, 182 F.4th 1314 (11th Cir. 2026). Rather, the inquiry turns on whether the proposed use is “reasonable and probable” or “too risky to qualify” (TOT Property Holdings, 1 F.4th at 1369). Quoting the seminal Supreme Court decision in Olson v. United States, 292 U.S. 246 (1934), the court emphasized: “[T]he Supreme Court ‘instructed that “[t]he highest and most profitable use for which the property is adaptable and needed or likely to be needed in the reasonably near future,” while not itself “the measure of value,” was relevant to the “extent that the prospect for such use affects the market value.”’” A use claiming a higher value than existing use requires both “closeness in time” and “reasonable probability” (Hilborn v. Commissioner, 85 T.C. 677 (1985)). Furthermore, an existing use is legally presumed to be the property’s highest and best use absent compelling proof to the contrary (United States v. Buhler, 305 F.2d 319 (5th Cir. 1962); Ranch Springs, 164 T.C. at 136). Crucially, the court reiterated from Boltar, L.L.C. v. Commissioner, 136 T.C. 326 (2011), that highest and best use is merely an element of fair market value and cannot override the essential requirement that a hypothetical willing buyer would actually purchase the real estate for the indicated value. In the specific context of mineral properties, the court invoked established Fourth and Tenth Circuit jurisprudence: “Where the asserted highest and best use of property is the extraction of minerals, the presence of the mineral in a commercially exploitable amount and the existence of a market ‘that would justify its extraction in the reasonably foreseeable future’ must be shown. ‘There must be some objective support for the future demand, including volume and duration. Mere physical adaptability to a use does not establish a market.’” (J L Minerals, LLC v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-93 (quoting Esgar Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-35, aff’d, 744 F.3d 648 (10th Cir. 2014); United States v. 69.1 Acres of Land, 942 F.2d 290 (4th Cir. 1991); United States v. Whitehurst, 337 F.2d 765 (4th Cir. 1964))). Petitioner contended that the highest and best use of the Riddle Property before the easement was an operating limestone aggregate quarry, sponsoring expert reports from Gregory Gold (mining engineer), Michael Stine (mineral valuation/market analyst), and Kyle Catlett (real estate appraiser). Respondent countered through reports from Brian Groff (mining engineer), Neal Rigby (mining feasibility), Shannon Rentz (geologist/market analyst), and Michael Rogers (real estate appraiser), maintaining that the highest and best use was limited residential, agriculture, silviculture, and recreation, with potential for future mining. The Tax Court systematically examined and exposed severe technical flaws in petitioner’s expert submissions: Petitioner’s mining engineer, Mr. Gold, projected that a hypothetical mine would extract 27,963,169 tons of limestone over a 30-year mine life. However, his report relied on an initial geotechnical assessment containing data from only two exploratory borings. Both borings were drilled outside Mr. Gold’s proposed mining pit area, leaving zero core testing data from the actual proposed excavation zone. Respondent’s expert, Mr. Groff, demonstrated that establishing geological continuity across limestone strata requires a minimum of three core samples drilled to the elevation of the pit floor to correlate formations, assess deleterious interbeds, and define orientation. Furthermore, Mr. Gold allocated a mere 4 to 5 acres for the on-site processing plant and stockpiles to handle a projected 1.5 million tons per year. Mr. Groff surveyed six active, competing limestone quarries in the surrounding market, revealing that active quarries producing between 248,812 and 748,599 tons required plant sites ranging from 14 to over 20 acres. Mr. Gold’s proposed plant footprint was roughly one-third the size of the smallest operational quarry plant in the region, rendering the operational mine plan physically unworkable. Petitioner’s market analyst, Mr. Stine, constructed an income model that assigned an arbitrary 15% market capture rate to Morgan County based strictly on road mileage to county borders, rather than distance to actual population centers or construction demand nodes. Respondent’s geologist, Ms. Rentz, demonstrated that existing regional quarry production reported by the Alabama Department of Labor exceeded Mr. Stine’s total market demand estimate by more than 100%, proving that regional supply was already abundant and that no unmet market demand existed for a new entrant. Moreover, petitioner’s own experts contradicted one another: Mr. Catlett estimated total 2017 market demand at 6,336,000 to 8,173,000 tons, whereas Mr. Stine estimated total demand at only 4,406,130 tons. The court remarked that this wide divergence among petitioner’s own experts failed to inspire confidence. Compounding these market deficiencies, respondent’s expert Dr. Rigby established that the market within a 25-to-50-mile radius was already dominated by large, well-capitalized, integrated producers (such as Vulcan Materials Co.) that operated multi-site logistics networks, owned downstream ready-mix concrete and asphalt plants, and enjoyed rail and barge access. A hypothetical greenfield quarry on the landlocked Riddle Property possessed no rail or barge access, no downstream integration, and inferior proximity to growth corridors, placing it at an insurmountable delivered-cost disadvantage. Mr. Catlett attempted to perform a “check of reasonableness” on the financial feasibility of a quarry by calculating the net present value of cash flows over its initial six years. However, trial testimony revealed a computational error in Mr. Catlett’s model; upon correction, the net present value of the first six years of operations was negative $778,618. Mr. Catlett conceded under cross-examination that negative cash flow indicates an operation is not financially feasible. Finally, the court highlighted that the syndication PPM explicitly warned that developing a quarry would require substantial additional capital and was unsuited for investors seeking cash returns. The record was devoid of any evidence that the promoters or syndication investors ever contemplated mining as a genuine commercial endeavor. Concluding that petitioner failed to demonstrate “closeness in time” or “reasonable probability” of mining operations, the Tax Court adopted Mr. Rogers’s conclusion that the pre-easement highest and best use was limited residential, agricultural, silvicultural, and recreational use, with potential for future mining. Having determined that commercial limestone mining was not the highest and best use, the court addressed petitioner’s valuation methodology. Mr. Catlett asserted an unencumbered property value of $28,030,000 ($121,227 per acre) using the “owner-operator” DCF income method, purportedly confirmed by a royalty DCF method. The Tax Court flatly rejected the application of the DCF income method to value raw, unimproved real estate: “Income-based methods are not favored when valuing vacant land with no income-producing history because they are inherently speculative and unreliable.” Judge Kerrigan reiterated a fundamental valuation principle established across an extensive line of Tax Court jurisprudence (Piton Holdings, LLC v. Commissioner, 167 T.C. (July 15, 2026); Ranch Springs, LLC v. Commissioner, 164 T.C. 93 (2025); Beaverdam Creek Holdings, LLC v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2025-53): “Previously, we have held that the use of a DCF method is erroneous where it equates the value of raw land with the net present value of a hypothetical limestone business conducted on the land.” The court noted that this error is recurrent in syndicated conservation easement cases: “This Court has addressed and rejected repeatedly the use of the income method to value mineral properties with no income-producing history in conservation easement cases. . . . A knowledgeable buyer would simply not pay the entire projected value of a business for one of the assets needed to conduct the business.” Citing Whitehouse Hotel Ltd. Partnership v. Commissioner, 139 T.C. 304 (2012), the court stressed that capitalization methods depend upon a historical track record of operational earnings, revenue, and expenses. A DCF model applied to raw land is acutely vulnerable to manipulation because relatively minor variations in discount rates, pricing, production, or cost assumptions generate massive distortions in the terminal output. Here, Mr. Catlett assumed perpetual year-over-year sales increases culminating in 1.48 million tons annually by 2046, despite empirical evidence showing that competing regional quarries averaged 300,000 to 400,000 tons and experienced flat or declining production trends. Mr. Groff proved that capping the Riddle Property’s annual production at 460,000 tons drove the model’s net present value below zero. The court dismissed petitioner’s DCF as a “‘rosy projection[]’ that contemplates only success.” In stark contrast to petitioner’s income modeling, respondent’s expert appraiser, Michael Rogers, utilized the comparable sales approach to establish the unencumbered before-value. Under the principle of substitution, “the value of a property can be estimated at the cost of acquiring an equally desirable substitute” (Mill Road 36 Henry, LLC v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-129, aff’d, 2026 WL 2443948 (11th Cir. 2026); North Donald LA Property, LLC v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-19). Mr. Rogers identified six arm’s-length sales of unimproved acreage in Morgan County occurring between 2014 and 2018. These sales exhibited unadjusted prices ranging from $1,839 to $2,911 per acre, with an average price of $2,506 per acre. Accounting for physical and locational attributes, Mr. Rogers concluded an unencumbered value of $2,898 per acre, arriving at a pre-easement fair market value of $670,000. County tax assessor records corroborated this baseline: out of 28 vacant land sales exceeding 50 acres between 2014 and 2019, 27 sold for prices between $1,458 and $11,089 per acre (with the single highest sale at $21,934 per acre reflecting a municipal acquisition for a public high school). The court emphatically applied the principle of substitution: “A willing buyer would not have paid roughly $121,000 per acre for nonunique land when the price per acre for substitute properties was less than $3,000 per acre.” The court found compelling verification for Mr. Rogers’s valuation in the September 2017 transaction wherein Freeman Five contributed Tracts One, Two, and Three (880.56 acres) to Quorum Holdings and sold 98% of the entity’s membership interests to Longleaf for $2,236,175. Grossing up this arm’s-length transaction to 100% established an implied market value of $2,281,811, or $2,591 per acre—completed barely three months prior to the conservation contribution. The court rejected petitioner’s attempt to disregard this sale, relying on Eleventh Circuit authority (TOT Property Holdings, 1 F.4th at 1371; Savannah Shoals II, 182 F.4th at 1332 n.15) establishing that recent arm’s-length purchases of partnership interests holding real property are “‘overwhelmingly significant’ evidence” of market value: “The purchase of an interest in a partnership can be ‘reflective of the price that the market would pay for [a property], especially when the ownership interest was nearly 100% and the only asset held by the [p]artnership was the [property] itself.’” While Mr. Rogers considered this sale as a market benchmark, petitioner’s appraiser completely failed to reconcile his $121,227-per-acre conclusion with the $2,591-per-acre price paid by his own syndication sponsor, speculating without basis that the seller must have lacked market knowledge. The court firmly rejected this assertion, finding that James Freeman Sr. was a highly experienced real estate trader. Further demonstrating the absurdity of petitioner’s valuation, the court examined a subsequent August 2024 transaction where Hollingshead Materials, LLC, acquired a 946.39-acre parcel in Morgan County with active mining intent. Despite possessing prime frontage on the Tennessee River—granting vital low-cost water barge transportation—the parcel sold for $8,250,000, or $8,717 per acre, representing a tiny fraction of petitioner’s $121,227-per-acre claim. Adopting Mr. Rogers’s valuation, the Tax Court synthesized the before-and-after easement valuation under Treasury Regulation Section 1.170A-14(h)(3)(i): Subtracting the stipulated encumbered after-value of $345,000 from the unencumbered before-value of $670,000, the court held that the allowable charitable contribution deduction for the conservation easement was $325,000—a reduction of over 99.2% from the $44,995,000 deduction claimed on Form 1065. Under IRC Section 6662(a) and (b)(3), an accuracy-related penalty of 20% applies to underpayments attributable to substantial valuation misstatements, defined under Section 6662(e)(1)(A) as claimed values equal to 150% or more of the correct amount. Under Section 6662(h)(1) and (h)(2)(A)(i), the penalty rate increases to 40% in the case of a “gross valuation misstatement,” triggered when the claimed value exceeds 200% of the correct amount. Riddle claimed an easement value of $44,995,000 on its partnership return, whereas the court determined the correct fair market value to be $325,000. Because the claimed deduction exceeded the correct value by nearly 13,845%—far surpassing the 200% threshold—the misstatement was categorized as gross. For tax practitioners evaluating potential defenses, the court’s penalty holding underscores critical statutory constraints: Inapplicability of Reasonable Cause: Under IRC Section 6664(c)(1), taxpayers may generally raise a defense of reasonable cause and good faith to avoid Section 6662 penalties. However, Section 6664(c)(3) explicitly bars the reasonable cause defense in cases involving gross valuation misstatements of charitable contribution property. As Judge Kerrigan observed, citing Chandler v. Commissioner, 142 T.C. 279 (2014): “Since the overstatement was ‘gross,’ the reasonable cause defense is not available.” Inapplicability of Adequate Disclosure: Petitioner argued that adequate disclosure under IRC Section 6662(d)(2)(B) precluded the imposition of the penalty. The court dismissed this argument out of hand, reiterating that the statutory text of Section 6662 restricts the disclosure exception to substantial understatements of income tax under Section 6662(d), providing no relief against valuation misstatements under subsections (e) or (h) (Piton Holdings, 167 T.C., slip op. at 52). Constitutional and Administrative Challenges Dismissed: Petitioner additionally raised a constitutional challenge arguing that the Supreme Court’s decision in Trump v. Slaughter, 146 S. Ct. 2283 (2026), undermined the Tax Court’s authority and guaranteed a Seventh Amendment jury trial prior to penalty assessments. The Tax Court rejected this argument, noting that Slaughter expressly disclaimed addressing tenure protections for judges of non-Article III courts, leaving the court’s jurisdiction and penalty adjudication authority fully intact. The Tax Court entered decision under Rule 155, sustaining the $325,000 easement valuation and imposing the non-waivable 40% gross valuation misstatement penalty under Section 6662(h). title: Obituary for Albert V. Silva - Waitt Funeral Home
content:
We would like to offer our sincere support to anyone coping with grief. Enter
                    your email below for our complimentary daily grief messages. Messages run for up to one year and you
                    can stop at any time. Your email will not be used for any other purpose. Albert V. Silva, 82, of Holbrook, formerly of Brockton, passed away peacefully at home on November 9, 2026. A native of  Stoughton, he was the son of the late Maria Isabelle (Borges) and Manuel Silva. Al was a longtime custodian for the Brockton Public Schools, retiring after 25 years of employment. Al was dedicated to his family and cherished the memories made throughout the years, especially with his grandchildren, of whom he was proud. Known as the life of any party, he loved bringing family together at his home for celebrations, big or small. He enjoyed being by the ocean and was a snowbird with his wife Kathy, spending winters in North Fort Myers. Al loved Christmas and was always back home in Massachusetts to spend the holiday with his entire family. Al also enjoyed playing the accordion. Al was the beloved husband of Kathleen A. (Walsh) Silva for 58 beautiful years; loving father of Michael Silva of Florida, Albert Silva Jr. and his wife Jill of Brockton, Jeffrey Silva of Wilmington, and the late Brian Silva; devoted grandfather of Justin and his wife Hannah, Alison, Brian, Cori, and Brooke; great-grandfather of Hallie; brother of the late Manuel, Alfred, John, and Joseph Silva, and Mary Fahey; and an uncle of many nieces and nephews. Al was also the best friend of the late Richard “Dickie” Carney and his widow Paula of Holbrook. He will be fondly remembered and greatly missed. All are welcome to calling hours on Sunday, November 15th from 2-5 p.m. at Waitt Funeral Home, 850 North Main St., Brockton, his funeral service on Monday, November 16th at 10 a.m. at Waitt Funeral Home and burial at Melrose Cemetery, Brockton. title: ‘The many v the money’ should frame the next US Congress - The Guardian
content: If Democrats want to keep the blue wave going into 2028, they have to take on the billionaire class Welcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Last week, Judd Legum shined a spotlight on the role of dark money in US elections. Today’s edition was written by Naomi Klein, Guardian US columnist and author of End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, co-written with Astra Taylor. To see the battle lines of the post-midterm era in sharp relief, look to Texas. Just two days after her earthquake victory as the governor-elect, Gina  informed reporters that she had already asked the parks and wildlife department to freeze a proposal to sell 1,300 acres (525 hectares) in a state park to SpaceX until she is sworn into her new office. The department complied with her request. The Boca Chica state park is next door to Starbase, Elon Musk’s rocket launch facility and company town. That makes the park’s beaches and protected lands – a refuge for shore birds and sea turtles – the ideal location for SpaceX to expand. “These are our beaches we’re talking about. I mean, selling our beach to Elon Musk is just something that is almost unimaginable,” Hinojosa told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “It’s unacceptable. Our beaches are enshrined in our Texas constitution as being free and open to the people of Texas.” This was not about shutting down “Elon Musk and his companies”, she went on, “but it has to be on our terms. It cannot be just running over the people of Texas. And that’s what changes now that I will be governor.” When Hinojosa’s clips circulated on X, she was roundly mocked by Musk’s many fans: imagine valuing some “empty beaches” more than the need for ocean-front launchpads to the stars! Imagine caring more about some lowly birds than Musk’s hulking, phallic, silver rockets! She must be a [insert vomitorium of misogynistic, racist and ableist slurs here]. Musk, his boys and bots predicted, will just pick up his expensive toys and move them to still-Republican Louisiana or Florida, leaving economic carnage in his wake. So far, Hinojosa seems unmoved. In Texas, she and Senator-elect James Talarico shaped their campaigns as battles of the many v the money, a vertical struggle pitting the vast majority of Texans, struggling to get by, against the increasingly concentrated wealth at the top – perfectly embodied by the man flooding their democracy with cash. As Talarico reminded an audience of supporters in Austin last month: “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator.” The richest man in the world didn’t get his senator, or his governor, as the early clash over Boca Chica state park makes clear. What he did get – or rather, help produce – is an America polarized around a new political axis. On one side are ultrarich tech oligarchs, whose wealth is tethered to dreams of merging with machines and becoming multiplanetary, no matter the cost to our multispecies planet. On the other side are regular people, with human needs for things such as clean air, fresh water and healthcare – maybe even a day off at a public park – and who increasingly find themselves competing over these basics with sprawling datacentres and rocket launchers. The oligarchs in this battle have no loyalty to the nations, states and cities that helped them grow their enormous wealth, thus the threats that Musk will soon ditch Texas if its newly elected representatives dare to keep their promises to voters (just as he dumped California and Canada before that). If all else fails, maybe he will join his friend Peter Thiel in Argentina, which Javier Milei is rapidly turning into techno-libertarian laboratory (Interestingly, Tesla just launched an Argentine division.) double quotation markThe oligarchs in this battle seem to have no loyalty to the nations, states and cities that helped them grow their enormous wealth. In sharp contrast, the masses of people in this battle, regardless of their political leanings, tend to be attached to where they live – to its cities, towns, public lands and to the only planet that we know of suited to human life. This is as true in Texas as it is in Tirana, Albania, where, under the banner of the “flamingo revolution” citizens have been in revolt for months against a different set of oligarchs who laid claim to a different beloved wildlife refuge for their private benefit. In our book End Times Fascism, Astra Taylor and I characterize these as fights between “the leavers v the stayers” – and we make the case that they increasingly define our age. You can see these fault lines running through a great many of the hot-button issues that animated and energized this election cycle. There were the many ballot measures to tax the super-rich to pay for basic services, and entirely predictable tantrums from billionaires who threatened to pick and leave rather than pay up. There was the muscular, national backlash against artificial intelligence and datacenters, which focused on the ways this latest (final?) capitalist stage is devouring art, literature, incomes, lands, energy and wellbeing. (As the Guardian reported, “Voters approved nearly every datacenter moratorium that was on the ballot, dozens in total.”) The commitment to place, and to one another, was equally evident in the rage at the US war-of-choice in Iran, and at Israel’s genocide in Gaza, with many winning candidates including Abdul El-Sayed consistently stressing that the money being spent to kill children far away should be used to care for children at home, and that all children are equally deserving of life and opportunities. Bernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk. Similar dynamics were there, too, in the revolt against ICE: As Minnesota’s Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said in her victory speech, the movement that lifted her to power all began when Minnesotans decided to stand up to “masked goons shooting our neighbors”. And the faultlines were clearest of all in the white-hot anger at the legalized corruption at the heart of the US political system, now widely understood as the wellspring producing all the other depravities. Writing in this space one month ago, Rebecca Solnit astutely characterized the midterms as “a referendum on the GOP’s alignment with tech overlords over the public they’re meant to serve”. Well, the results are in and they could scarcely be more decisive. The complicating factor, however, is that it is not only the GOP that is aligned with the tech overlords and their anti-human, anti-Earth agenda. Plenty of powerful Democrats have chosen to underwrite their political campaigns and their personal wealth portfolios by entangling themselves with the very individuals and corporations their voters just roundly and unequivocally rejected. Shamefully, the campaign to defeat a California ballot measure that would have imposed a much-needed, one-time 5% tax on billionaires – one of few places where tech oligarchs clocked a victory last week – was only successful because powerful Democrats including outgoing governor (and presidential hopeful) Gavin Newsom sided with the billionaires (as did the incoming governor). Meanwhile, several Senate Democrats have joined with Republicans to push through a sweeping bill in the current lame-duck Congress that would dismantle a host of environmental protections and be a bonanza for fossil fuel companies and the datacentres that burn them. This kind of betrayal is the surest path for Democrats to turn their historic midterm victories into entirely predictable defeats before the highly consequential 2028 presidential election. In Texas, Hinojosa is showing a better way. By picking an early fight pitting public beaches against Musk’s private rockets, she is telling voters which side she is on – the side of life, not machines; the side of staying, not leaving. That is how the Democrats just won, and it is their path to continue winning. Follow them on Substack and elsewhere: Stacey Abrams, Robert Reich, Paul Krugman, Naomi Klein, Mehdi Hasan, Bernie Sanders, Rebecca Solnit, Katie Phang, Judd Legum, Wajahat Ali, Margaret Sullivan and Charles Blow.

title: The Upshot of Epic Tech v. Pen-Tech: The Presumption of Validity Is Not a Pre-Suit Investigation - IPWatchdog
content: “[After Epic Tech], the infringement comparison and the validity assessment are now two separate pre-suit obligations, and a record that answers the first says nothing about the second.” Epic Tech’s U.S. Patent No. 8,545,317, directed to a networked electronic sweepstakes system, issued in October 2013. Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank came eight months later. Over the next several years, the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) rejected claims in three related Epic Tech applications under Section 101, having already found claims in two of them patentably indistinct from the ‘317 claims, and Epic Tech abandoned all three. A district court in Texas then held claims of the sibling ‘315 patent ineligible. In June 2020, six years after Alice, Epic Tech sued Pen-Tech Associates on the ‘317 patent. The firm that had been prosecuting the rejected applications filed the complaint. The district court held the asserted claims ineligible on summary judgment but denied Rule 11 sanctions and fees under Sections  285,  1927, and its inherent power, crediting Epic Tech’s “good faith, pre-suit investigation” and the claim chart its counsel had prepared. On September 30, 2026, in a precedential opinion by Chief Judge Moore, the Federal Circuit vacated all four rulings. Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc., No. 25-1624 (Fed. Cir. Sept. 30, 2026). The reasoning turned on a distinction most pre-suit investigations ignore. The district court’s reliance on the infringement investigation, the panel wrote, “does not explain why sanctions were unjustified under Pen-Tech’s notice theory centered on validity.” Those facts “may bear on whether Epic Tech reasonably investigated infringement before filing suit, but they do not address the distinct question of whether Epic Tech should have investigated validity.” And in the sentence that will appear in every fee motion involving a pre-Alice software patent: “it does not suffice for Epic Tech or its counsel to rely only on the presumption of validity when faced with multiple indicators that these claims were unpatentable under § 101.” The panel was careful about what it did not decide. It did not hold that Rule 11 was violated, and it did not say when notice of potential invalidity makes continued assertion of a presumptively valid patent unreasonable. It held only that a district court must engage with the question. The practical consequence is the same. The infringement comparison and the validity assessment are now two separate pre-suit obligations, and a record that answers the first says nothing about the second. Practitioners sometimes talk about “the pre-suit investigation standard” as though there were one. There are at least three regimes, and until Epic Tech the Federal Circuit’s Rule 11 cases were almost entirely about infringement. Rule 11(b)(3) is the familiar starting point. In patent cases, counsel must at minimum interpret the asserted claims and compare them to the accused device before filing. View Engineering, Inc. v. Robotic Vision Systems, Inc., 208 F.3d 981, 986 (Fed. Cir. 2000). Q-Pharma, Inc. v. Andrew Jergens Co., 360 F.3d 1295, 1302 (Fed. Cir. 2004), made the presence of an infringement analysis the key factor, and Intamin, Ltd. v. Magnetar Technologies Corp., 483 F.3d 1328 (Fed. Cir. 2007), held that a patentee need not always buy and dissect the accused product. Every one of those cases asked whether the patentee had compared claims to a product. None asked whether the patentee had considered whether the claims were valid. Epic Tech adds that question to Rule 11, which is where it reaches counsel directly. Section 285 asks something broader. Under Octane Fitness, an exceptional case is one that “stands out from others” on the totality of the circumstances, and pre-suit diligence is a factor rather than a test. Bayer CropScience AG v. Dow AgroSciences LLC, 851 F.3d 1302, 1307 (Fed. Cir. 2017). The validity inquiry has lived here for a decade. In Rothschild Connected Devices Innovations, LLC v. Guardian Protection Services, Inc., 858 F.3d 1383 (Fed. Cir. 2017), the Federal Circuit reversed a fee denial because the district court ignored the patentee’s “willful ignorance of the prior art” after a safe-harbor letter arrived with anticipating references attached. The same opinion rejected the idea that fees require Rule 11-sanctionable conduct, quoting Octane: sanctionable conduct “is not the appropriate benchmark.” Chief Judge Moore repeated that holding this August in VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc., No. 24-2226 (Fed. Cir. Aug. 19, 2026). Section 1927 and inherent-power sanctions require bad faith or recklessness and are governed by regional circuit law. They are the regime patentees fear and the one least often triggered. The exposure that matters in ordinary litigation is Section 285, which needs no bad-faith finding, and now Rule 11, which needs no fee motion from a prevailing party to be raised. The division of labor among the three has a practical consequence. A patentee can clear Rule 11 on infringement and still lose on Section 285 for validity, as Rothschild did. After Epic Tech, it can also lose on Rule 11 for validity while holding a perfectly good claim chart. Epic Tech did not invent the idea that an issued patent can be too weak to assert. In Finnavations LLC v. Payoneer, Inc., No. 18-444 (D. Del. Mar. 18, 2019), Judge Andrews awarded § 285 fees after a § 101 dismissal and rejected the argument that the examiner’s allowance over four § 101 rejections excused the patentee from assessing eligibility itself. Issuance “cannot and should not be a license to sue with abandon,” he wrote, and “any reasonable patent attorney with an understanding of Section 101 law could have predicted the outcome.” The point generalizes beyond § 101. In WPEM, LLC v. SOTI Inc., 2020 WL 555545 (E.D. Tex. Feb. 4, 2020), aff’d, No. 20-1483 (Fed. Cir. Dec. 9, 2020) (nonprecedential), Chief Judge Gilstrap awarded fees because the patentee had built its case on the user manual for version 11 of the accused software without asking whether version 10, which predated the patent and was linked from the same manual, was itself prior art. The court found that WPEM “conducted absolutely no pre-filing investigation into the validity or enforceability” of its patent, and that “even the most cursory” one would have found the problem. What Epic Tech adds is the appellate statement that this failure is a Rule 11 question, not only a Section 285 one, and a description of what counts as notice. None of the three indicators in Epic Tech came from the defendant. That is the part of the opinion worth reading twice. The first was Alice itself. The patent was examined under pre-Alice law and asserted six years after the law changed. The district court never addressed whether that alone put Epic Tech on notice, and the panel treated the omission as reversible. The point is not confined to software. Any claim examined before a Supreme Court or en banc decision reset the governing test carries the same question. A functional genus claim allowed before Amgen v. Sanofi is the life-sciences version of a software claim allowed before Alice. The second was the family’s own prosecution history. The Section 101 rejections of indistinct claims in the continuations were office actions issued to Epic Tech’s own counsel. The district court brushed them aside on the ground that later prosecution history cannot limit an earlier patent’s claims. The panel pointed out that Pen-Tech had never argued claim scope; it argued notice. An examiner’s rejection of claims the USPTO itself called patentably indistinct from the asserted claims is a statement about how the asserted claims would fare under current law. It sits in the file wrapper. The third was the sibling patent’s loss in another district. The district court dismissed Fusion Skill because “the issues were not the exact same.” The panel’s answer: “the issues need not be identical to provide notice of potential invalidity.” A related patent’s adverse ruling is in the patentee’s own docket. The lesson for anyone who prosecutes as well as litigates is uncomfortable. The office action rejecting the continuation is notice to the litigator. The intervening Supreme Court decision is notice. The sibling patent’s loss is notice. Before filing, the question is not whether the patent issued, but whether these claims would issue today, and whether anything in the family’s history since issuance suggests the answer has changed. Each item corresponds to a failure that has drawn fees or sanctions. Epic Tech is about the law and the prosecution record. The same court has spent the past year saying the same thing about the patentee’s commercial files. In VDPP, fees were affirmed against a patentee that sued on an expired patent and sought pre-suit damages without checking the marking obligations in its own settlement licenses. In Viavi Solutions v. Platinum Optics Technology (Fed. Cir. Sept. 8, 2026) (nonprecedential), fees ran from the day a sworn declaration refuted a theory the patentee had built on a sample it had already licensed. Those cases are a subject for another day. The common thread is the one Epic Tech makes explicit: the evidence that should have stopped the suit was in the patentee’s possession before the complaint was filed. Q-Pharma still states the floor, and Epic Tech did not raise it; the panel decided no sanctions question and set no threshold for when notice of invalidity makes assertion unreasonable. What it did decide is enough to change the file. A claim chart answers one question. A court that denies fees on that record now has to explain why, with Alice in the reporters and Section 101 rejections in the family’s own file wrapper, the claim still had a reasonable chance of success.
