title: Old Vic 2027 season to feature Damian Lewis in a ‘provocative’ Henry V and Milly Alcock as Miss Julie - The Guardian
content: Rupert Goold begins his tenure as artistic director with a version of Shakespeare’s history play, followed by shows starring Supergirl’s Alcock and Arinzé Kene Damian Lewis is to play Henry V at the Old Vic in London in the first production under the theatre’s new artistic director, Rupert Goold. Goold will direct what is billed as a “provocative” version of Shakespeare’s history play that challenges “what makes a leader a legend”. It will be Lewis’s first major theatre role since he starred in The Goat, or Who Is Sylvia? almost 10 years ago. He has previously played Romeo and Hamlet on stage, as well as appearing in Cymbeline and Much Ado About Nothing for the Royal Shakespeare Company. Henry V, with a set design by Miriam Buether, will have its first performance on 26 January. It will be followed by a version of August Strindberg’s Miss Julie, adapted and directed by Rebecca Frecknall, the Old Vic’s new associate director. The adaptation, Julie, was originally produced by the celebrated Internationaal Theater Amsterdam, with whom the Old Vic will pursue an ongoing artistic partnership. Milly Alcock (Supergirl) will take the lead role. In the summer, Goold will direct a revival of Stephen Sondheim and John Weidman’s satirical musical Assassins, about historical attempts to murder the president of the US. Arinzé Kene will then star as a wronged horse-dealer in Kohlhaas, based on a novella by Marco Baliani and Remo Rostagno, translated and directed by Omar Elerian. Kohlhaas was staged at Brighton festival earlier this year, where it received a five-star Guardian review. Goold said his first season “speaks to the Old Vic’s rich history of classical theatre, European repertoire and musical revivals” and that he hopes to draw on its “storied legacy of sensational acting in groundbreaking and accessible productions”. The Old Vic, a not-for-profit theatre that is a charity, “has always sat between the subsidised and commercial sectors, dancing to its own distinctive tune” he added, and is “innately a maverick playhouse”. A new ticketing scheme, Old Vic New Rush, will offer front row tickets for £20 for the first five previews of every main-house show. Laura Stevenson, executive director of the theatre, said the scheme was part of their ambition “to be a welcoming place for people of all ages to experience the joy and power of theatre”. Goold joined the Old Vic after his tenure at the Almeida theatre, now run by Dominic Cooke. London theatre is undergoing a fresh period of leadership change, with Michelle Terry announcing her departure from Shakespeare’s Globe and Tom Littler leaving the Orange Tree theatre to run the Arts theatre in Cambridge. title: Phil Mickelson's Gulfstream V: Why golf's biggest stars fly privately - Newsbug.info
content: Phil Mickelson of Hyflyers gc on seventeenth tee box during day one of LIV Golf South Africa at The Club at Steyn City on March 19, 2026 in Johannesburg. Phil "Lefty" Mickelson captivated golf fans for three decades with his magician-like short game, ranking eighth on the all-time PGA Tour victories list with 45 wins. The six-time Major winner made history as the oldest major champion in golf history, and is now taking a prolonged break from a full tournament schedule. Beyond gathering titles and winning championships, Lefty is also one of the richest golfers in the world, with an estimated net worth of over $400 million. And like any professional golfer who takes himself seriously, he owns a small sports car collection and a private jet. Jettly, an on-demand private jet charter marketplace and membership platform, takes a look at Lefty's Gulfstream V, analyzing its standout features, and provides a deeper understanding of why so many celebrity golfers fly privately. In true celebrity golf lifestyle fashion, Phil Mickelson had his own private jet, a $40 million Gulfstream V. Unlike other sports celebrities, Lefty was loyal to his first aircraft and kept it for about 20 years. The star golfer is also a licensed pilot. He grew up surrounded by aviation: His father (his first golf teacher) was a former naval aviator and commercial airline pilot. So, growing up, young Phil learned to respect and love both planes and golf. Still, once he made it big and became an aircraft owner, Lefty left flying his Gulfstream V to professional pilots and simply enjoyed the comfort. The Gulfstream V is known for ultra-long-range capability (around 6,500 nautical miles), and the jet owned by our golfer was customized with full sleeping berths, two lavish bathrooms (rumored to feature gold-plated fixtures), and custom galley spaces for catering. During his peak touring years, the jet was instrumental for Phil's comfort and well-being. The option to fly privately made it easy to zip between tournament stops and his family home in California. It was a way to maintain family life while also navigating a demanding tournament schedule. After about 20 years of being a private jet owner, Mickelson decided it was time to give it up. So, in 2021, he sold his Gulfstream V and partnered with a private jet charter service that offers flight subscription programs. This move is quite unprecedented in celebrity aviation, where stars may change aircraft, but rarely give them up altogether. When asked about his decision, Lefty explained that owning a jet of this size full-time is stressful and costly. Despite the convenience and comfort of having an aircraft at the ready, full aircraft ownership comes with major operational headaches like crew scheduling, hangar fees, costly repairs, and lengthy maintenance jobs. When you choose fractional ownership or a subscription program, all these problems go away. Travelers get the same level of comfort and flexibility without the headaches of ownership. In sports travel, it is quite common to fly privately, but when it comes to golf, it's practically a given. That said, not all top golfers own a business aircraft. Besides Tiger Woods, who owns a Gulfstream G550, only a small handful of top pro golfers are full-time owners. But given the choice, almost all elite golfers will choose a private jet over commercial flights. Here's why: The first argument for flying private is convenience. Then, it's comfort. Having an entire plane at your and your team's disposal is pretty neat. There is room to talk strategy, analyze previous performances, or have a relaxing chat with advisors. There is also room for sleeping comfortably or just resting, which is important for an elite athlete heading to a competition. Many times, golfing tournaments have tight schedules, which makes it difficult to travel commercially. Sometimes, golfers will compete in Augusta, Georgia, on day one, and by day four, they have to be in Scotland, in St. Andrews. Keeping up with such a schedule while flying commercially would take a toll on any athlete's performance. Golf equipment is notoriously vulnerable to damage in transit, especially on commercial flights. While the clubs are engineered to withstand extreme forces when hitting a ball, the long graphite and steel shafts can be damaged by bending, dropping, or lateral pressure. Now imagine such sensitive luggage being loaded in a commercial airplane. The poor golfer won't be able to rest easy until they reach their destination, worrying about nightmare scenarios like damaged or stolen gear. In a private jet, all the bags and equipment are loaded with the utmost care. Some jets even have storage compartments for golf equipment, and some regional airports may offer ground transportation services for the equipment. Most major golf courses are far removed from major air hubs and the hustle and bustle of big cities. After landing at an international airport, getting there could mean hours of driving or multiple connections. That's not how an elite golfer should be spending their time right before competing in a tournament. Private jets are more convenient in this case because they can connect with smaller regional airports, closer to remote golf courses. Golf is still a sport steeped in luxury and old-world prestige. Country clubs look straight out of “The Great Gatsby,” and the ultra-rich often turn out to watch elite players (when they aren't playing themselves). Players who want to stand out must look the part. In this case, flying private is a powerful default status symbol, even when using a charter operator or a subscription service. It's a way to attract attention (other than through golf) and open the door toward networking and high-end sponsorships. Established golfers and up-and-coming stars alike tend to fly privately. It's more convenient, it fits better with tournament schedules, and it makes reaching remote courses effortless. However, when it comes to full aircraft ownership, most players take a page out of Phil Mickelson's book and opt for a less cumbersome solution. title: Study Identifies Thrombomodulin and Factor V as Optimal Deep Vein Thrombosis Biomarkers - Bioengineer.org
content: Study Identifies Thrombomodulin and Factor V as Optimal Deep Vein Thrombosis Biomarkers A computational genomics investigation combining genome-wide association study datasets with functional annotation scoring and tissue expression profiling has identified thrombomodulin and coagulation factor V as the most promising blood-based biomarker combination for assessing deep vein thrombosis risk. Deep vein thrombosis represents a major global health challenge involving the formation of pathogenic blood clots within deep venous structures, frequently culminating in life-threatening complications such as pulmonary embolism. Global epidemiological estimates indicate that venous thromboembolism accounts for more than ten million cases annually, with clinical incidence rising steeply in older demographics. In the United States alone, registry data from 2016 documented over 1.2 million individuals diagnosed with venous thromboembolism, among whom approximately forty percent presented with acute pulmonary embolism. Compounding this disease burden, the one-year mortality rate for pulmonary embolism has remained persistently high at 19.6 percent since 1999, highlighting the critical necessity for more reliable molecular indicators capable of identifying susceptible individuals prior to fatal thrombotic events. Contemporary clinical practice utilizes an array of conventional laboratory parameters to aid in the diagnosis and prognostication of deep vein thrombosis, yet a robust consensus on an optimal predictive biomarker panel has remained elusive. Routine diagnostic evaluations frequently measure basic hemostatic parameters, including prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and isolated coagulation factor activities, alongside intermediate indicators of coagulation cascade activation such as prothrombin fragment 1 plus 2, thrombin-antithrombin complexes, and soluble fibrin degradation products. Clinicians additionally monitor dynamic fibrinolytic regulators, including tissue plasminogen activator, plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, and plasma D-dimer, to gauge the delicate physiological equilibrium between intravascular clot generation and endogenous enzymatic breakdown. Endogenous circulating anticoagulant proteins, most notably antithrombin and regulatory cofactors, further contribute to this multifaceted hemostatic network. Despite decades of investigation into these circulating proteins, individual biomarker performance remains constrained by biological variability and non-specific elevation, prompting researchers to leverage large-scale genomic architectures to systematically prioritize robust, mechanistically anchored biomarker candidates. To establish a reproducible genetic foundation, the research team initiated their multi-stage computational workflow by interrogating established genomic repositories to isolate variants exhibiting robust statistical associations with venous thromboembolic traits. The researchers accessed the curated EBI-NHGRI Genome-Wide Association Study Catalog on October 24, 2024, extracting single-nucleotide polymorphisms linked to deep vein thrombosis and broader venous thromboembolism phenotypes. To filter out spurious associations and retain only variants demonstrating profound statistical rigor, the investigators enforced a stringent genome-wide significance threshold of p less than 5 multiplied by 10 to the negative eighth power. This initial data extraction yielded 689 single-nucleotide polymorphisms, of which 458 distinct variants successfully satisfied the rigorous genome-wide significance threshold. These validated variants served as the foundational genomic dataset for subsequent computational modeling, providing a reliable basis for dissecting the complex polygenic architecture that governs individual susceptibility to venous clot formation. Visualizing the extracted genomic associations through a genome-wide Manhattan plot revealed distinct chromosomal clusters where association signals peaked well above background variation. Pronounced regional peaks emerged across chromosomes 1, 4, 9, and 13, pointing directly toward discrete genomic loci harboring candidate risk genes and master regulatory elements involved in venous thrombogenesis. Among the most prominent peaks was the ABO gene locus situated on chromosome 9, a finding that aligns closely with established clinical observations regarding blood group antigens and differential venous thromboembolic risk profiles. The F5 gene locus on chromosome 1 also demonstrated substantial statistical significance, reflecting its well-characterized mechanistic function within the common pathway of blood coagulation. Additional peaks mapped to genomic regions containing ATP1B1, NME7, and FGB, reinforcing the polygenic foundation of the disease. Detailed evaluation guided the selection of the top forty single-nucleotide polymorphisms based on visual prominence and functional consistency, as empirical testing demonstrated that expanding candidate selection beyond these top forty variants yielded no additional genes satisfying their subsequent biological risk criteria. Because single-nucleotide polymorphisms frequently do not operate as isolated functional units and are often linked to adjacent regulatory variants through complex linkage disequilibrium patterns, the investigators expanded their initial genomic pool using advanced computational annotations. Utilizing HaploReg version 4.2, the team comprehensively mapped regulatory variants, chromatin states, and linked genomic sequences associated with the 458 genome-wide significant variants. The researchers specifically calibrated this computational expansion using linkage disequilibrium parameters derived from Asian population datasets, applying a stringent correlation threshold of r-squared greater than 0.80 to capture co-inherited variants within this demographic. This expansion broadened the scope of inquiry from the initial 458 significant markers to an expansive set of 4,430 linked single-nucleotide polymorphisms. In total, these mapped regulatory and coding variants mapped directly to 334 candidate genes, ensuring that subsequent prioritization steps captured the broader genomic landscape rather than overlooking critical functional loci through overly narrow variant isolation. To distill this large candidate pool into biologically actionable targets, the investigators implemented a multi-criteria functional annotation scoring framework adapted from established genetic prioritization models. The methodology evaluated each candidate gene against seven predefined biological risk criteria designed to integrate statistical, structural, and regulatory evidence: first, designation as a top-ranking gene derived from the most significant genome-wide association study signals; second, the presence of missense mutations located in high linkage disequilibrium with deep vein thrombosis variants at r-squared exceeding 0.80; third, documented whole-blood expression quantitative trait loci effects; fourth, verified involvement in biological processes classified under Gene Ontology terminology; fifth, mapped associations with defined cellular components; sixth, participation in recognized molecular functions; and seventh, verified overlap with primary immunodeficiency disease genes curated from the 2022 International Union of Immunological Societies reference registry. Gene Ontology terms were systematically evaluated using the WEB-based GEne SeT AnaLysis Toolkit, enabling the researchers to capture intersections between immunological modulation, endothelial physiology, and thrombotic risk. Applying a minimum functional annotation score cutoff of 3 successfully condensed the 334 candidate loci into a refined cohort of 28 biological risk genes directly implicated in the pathogenesis of deep vein thrombosis. Within this prioritized tier, IL6R achieved the highest aggregate functional annotation score of 6, reflecting extensive documentation across inflammatory signaling cascades that regulate endothelial activation and vascular hemostasis. The F5 and ABO genes each attained high functional annotation scores of 5, corroborating their central standing within both genomic association scans and classic prothrombotic pathways. Eleven additional loci attained functional annotation scores of 4, including the coagulation factors F2, F9, and F11, the contact system component KLKB1, the fibrinogen components FGA and FGB, the von Willebrand factor gene VWF, the metalloprotease ADAMTS13, the vascular and endothelial integrity regulator THBD, and the immune-modulating signaling intermediaries IL1RN and SH2B3. The presence of immune regulators alongside classical clotting cascades underscores the intricate pathophysiological crosstalk connecting vascular inflammation, immune surveillance, and thrombus propagation. To evaluate whether the 28 prioritized risk genes demonstrated coordinated biological activity, the researchers conducted systematic pathway enrichment analyses utilizing hypergeometric testing corrected by a false discovery rate threshold of 0.05. The computational enrichment results demonstrated marked statistical overrepresentation of these candidate genes within canonical pathways governing blood coagulation, the regulation of response to wounding, and tissue repair mechanisms. Specifically, a core subset of fifteen genes demonstrated significant enrichment within these physiological cascades: F5, F11, THBD, SH2B3, F9, KLKB1, PLCG2, FGB, VWF, FGA, ADAMTS13, F2, ST3GAL4, PROC, and PLEK. The prominent concentration of these genes within wound healing and hemostatic maintenance networks confirms that their genetic variation predominantly influences enzymatic balances controlling thrombin generation and fibrin clot stabilization, reinforcing their biological relevance to deep vein thrombosis. Building upon the pathway enrichment findings, the researchers executed network analysis leveraging the Enrichr platform to map direct gene-disease and gene-phenotype connections within the Jensen Disease and Human Phenotype Ontology databases. This network mapping isolated a central cluster of five primary genetic drivers that exhibited direct topological links to deep vein thrombosis and inherited thrombophilia phenotypes: F2, F5, F9, PROC, and THBD. Each of these five genes occupies a critical regulatory juncture within the coagulation and anticoagulation cascades. F2 and F5 encode prothrombin and coagulation factor V, respectively, which directly orchestrate prothrombinase complex assembly and fibrin deposition. Conversely, PROC encodes protein C, an essential circulating anticoagulant that degrades activated cofactors to prevent uncontrolled thrombosis. F9 encodes coagulation factor IX, an indispensable component of the intrinsic tenase complex, while THBD encodes thrombomodulin, an endothelial cell surface receptor that binds thrombin and dramatically accelerates protein C activation to maintain vascular patency. Although all five core genes demonstrated robust genetic and phenotypic associations with deep vein thrombosis, clinical utility requires that potential biomarkers be readily measurable in accessible biological specimens. To address this diagnostic requirement, the investigators evaluated bulk tissue gene expression profiles across whole blood and liver tissue using RNA-sequencing data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression Portal, alongside expression quantitative trait loci mapping via the haploR package in RStudio. The tissue profiling revealed a pronounced biological divergence among the five candidate genes. The coagulation factors F2 and F9, along with PROC, exhibited high baseline expression localized primarily within liver parenchyma, accompanied by low, highly variable expression levels in whole blood and an absence of documented whole-blood expression quantitative trait loci. This localized hepatic synthesis and blood-level fluctuation limit their practical suitability as direct circulating biomarkers. In stark contrast, both THBD and F5 exhibited robust, distributed expression within whole blood, coupled with confirmed whole-blood expression quantitative trait loci, confirming that circulating transcript levels reflect stable regulatory genetic variation. The biological convergence of thrombomodulin and factor V underscores a coherent molecular mechanism governing individual thrombotic susceptibility. Under healthy physiological conditions, endothelial thrombomodulin binds active thrombin, converting it from a procoagulant enzyme into an activator of protein C; activated protein C subsequently cleaves and inactivates activated factor V, suppressing further thrombin generation. Inherited variations in F5, such as the factor V Leiden mutation, confer resistance to activated protein C degradation, while variations in THBD impair endothelial anticoagulant signaling, tilting the hemostatic balance toward excessive thrombosis. The authors propose that because both THBD and F5 possess documented blood expression quantitative trait loci and measurable circulating profiles, they could be quantified via standardized plasma enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays to non-invasively assess thrombosis risk in clinical settings. The investigators caution that these two genes capture only a portion of the polygenic variation underlying deep vein thrombosis, noting that future translational studies must validate their predictive utility across multi-ethnic populations and evaluate their integration with established environmental risk factors such as patient age, physical immobility, and metabolic comorbidities. title: The Supreme Court Keeps Making Federal Agents Unaccountable. The New Congress Can Fix That - Balls and Strikes
content: Want more Balls & Strikes? Sign up for our free newsletter here. This article was published in partnership with Slate. On July 21, 2021, a riot erupted at the Federal Detention Center in Honolulu. During the chaos, at least four gang members jumped another incarcerated man, Kekai Watanabe, and brutally beat him with an improvised weapon—a combination lock placed in a sock. When Watanabe saw the prison nurse a few days later, he described his pain as a 10 on a 1-to-10 scale. But nurse Francis Nielsen told him to “stop being a crybaby.” Watanabe asked to go to the hospital. But Nielsen told him he was “not going.” For months, Watanabe begged for real medical attention. But Nielsen just gave him over-the-counter medication. The following year, an X-ray revealed that Watanabe’s tailbone was fractured, and bone chips had become lodged in the surrounding soft tissue. Only then did the prison agree that he could see a medical specialist. But the prison never made good on that agreement: Watanabe was released from federal custody in 2024 without ever receiving treatment. Today, Watanabe is still in extreme pain. And he is still seeking a remedy for the physical and legal injuries that he suffered during his incarceration. On Monday, the Supreme Court heard oral argument in Nielsen v. Watanabe, a case that will determine whether Watanabe and anyone else harmed by federal agents—whether in prisons, in immigration detention centers, or on the streets—can sue those agents for money damages, and hold them personally liable for violating constitutional rights. In theory, this should be an easy question. Over 50 years ago, in a case called Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents, the Supreme Court recognized that the Constitution inherently empowers people to sue federal agents who violate the rights that the Constitution protects. A few years later, the Court held that prison officials violate the Eighth Amendment’s protection against “cruel and unusual punishments” when they are “deliberately indifferent” to an incarcerated person’s “serious medical needs.” And by 1980, the Supreme Court explicitly put the two cases together, ruling in Carson v. Green that a grieving mother could bring a Bivens lawsuit against federal prison officials whose deliberate indifference to her son’s asthma attack caused his death. However, as its ideological makeup has lurched to the right, the Court has become increasingly hostile to attempts to hold government agents accountable for misconduct, no matter how egregious. In a 2022 majority opinion, for example, Justice Clarence Thomas stressed that courts may not extend Bivens to any “new contexts” if there is “any rational reason (even one)” to think that Congress was “better suited” to create a damages remedy itself. In doing so, Thomas both broke with precedent and slammed the courthouse doors on countless people harmed by federal agents. Thomas presented the Court’s capriciousness as humility, writing that “prescribing a cause of action” is almost always “a job for Congress, not the courts.” Yet it was not clear why redress for violating the Constitution should be dependent on Congress passing a statute. And it was all too clear that Congress—basically a vestigial organ in the modern era—was not about to pass any such statute anytime soon. But that was before last week’s midterm elections. In the new year, Democrats will have sizable majorities in both chambers of Congress. And Monday’s oral argument was colored both by awareness of what past congresses failed to do, and what the new Congress could actually do soon. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, for instance, was cautious when the attorney for the prison nurse pushed the court to move on from its incrementalist attacks on Bivens and Carlson and overrule the cases outright already. Kavanaugh pointed out that Congress has “left Bivens and Carlsonwhere they stood” for half a century, passing legislation “against that backdrop,” and that overruling the cases would be “pulling the rug out” from the legislature. The attorney, Lucas Walker, largely did not share Kavanaugh’s concern—and suggested that the justices didn’t really share it either. “This court has not hesitated to overrule past decisions,” said Walker, even though Congress “could have” chosen to legislatively override them. Furthermore, Walker said, if Congress does have a problem with the court ending Bivens, then Congress could pass a statute codifying the Bivens remedy. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson picked up on that answer in a back-and-forth with Department of Justice attorney Vivek Suri, who appeared as amicus supporting the prison nurse. Jackson asked Suri if he agreed that Congress could “respond to whatever we do here” and “reinstate the Carlson remedy” if the court were to overrule it. Suri said, “Of course.” Justice Elena Kagan then pressed Suri further still on a potential congressional response. “Typically,” Kagan said, the Justice Department considers whether “what we’re asking the court to do” is “essentially a dare to Congress.” Perhaps, then, the other branches of government can only say “Congress can do something” so many times before Congress calls their bluff and does something. “Have you thought about that?” Kagan asked. Suri replied that he could not “get into our internal deliberations” about “what we think Congress might or might not do.” For years, the Supreme Court has been invoking hypothetical congressional action as an excuse to ignore the very real harm that federal agents inflict on people like Watanabe. According to the court, they shouldn’t create consequences for constitutional violations, because if Congress wanted consequences, Congress could provide them. The incoming Congress has the chance to call the court’s bluff. Madiba K. Dennie is the Deputy Editor and Senior Contributor at Balls & Strikes, and a Fellow-in-Residence at the NYU Law Birnbaum Women’s Leadership Center. Her first book is The Originalism Trap: How Extremists Stole the Constitution and How We the People Can Take it Back. title: Xavier v. Detroit Mercy: Preview, matchups, and keys to the game - Yahoo Sports
content: There is a limited amount of information that can reliably be garnered from the amount of games played at this point in the season, and it's questionable whether or not that information will be accurate or even pertinent when March rolls around. A lot can change during the course of a college basketball campaign, and both attrition and development will change the composition and performance of virtually every roster during that time. Those disclaimers should serve as context when I tell you that Detroit Mercy is not a good team and this game will serve only as a counting stat in the Q4 column when resume time rolls around. Fresh off of a season in which they won just a single non-conference game against D1 competition, UDM lost by 61 to Marquette in their season opener on Friday. They peaked at 1.2% win probability by trailing just 9-8 before surrendering a 10-0 run in just over two minutes of game time. A 36-5 run that straddled the half functionally ended the game, as 36-5 runs tend to do. Pick a stat and it looks bad for them, but maybe the most notable is that they scored in just 6 of their 34 second half possessions. It was a destruction. Xavier, on the other hand, has been gorging on cupcakes. The Muskies brushed aside Mount St. Mary's in the opener and then outscored Eastern Michigan 65-35 after the second media timeout of the game to turn a slow start into a comfortable victory. Sterner tests lie ahead, but for the moment, X has been giving it to all takers while barely breaking a sweat. As might be expected of a team that lost by 60, the numbers aren't pretty for Detroit Mercy. They're a merely bad offensive rebounding team; the rest of the offensive side of the ledger is absolutely abysmal. They're in the bottom 10 of D1 in free throw rate, turnover rate, and EFG% as a team. They can't hit from inside or beyond the arc, and they're poor from the line. They had almost a quarter of their two-point shots blocked and played at a glacial pace. Just ugly ball. Defensively, it's not as bad, but it's still not good. They managed to keep Marquette off the line, though that appears to be through a lack of meaningful resistance rather than any real defensive nous. They somehow forced just 3 turnovers in a 67 possession game, which is honestly incredible. The rest of the numbers are also bad, but again, it's a one game sample. I think the biggest takeaway is that Marquette destroyed them and, if Xavier wants to compete near the top of the Big East this year, they need to do the same. Our famous players grid ™ will return when Joel is able to write more and clears up some of the coding in the grid. I'm an ideas man, I thrive on energy. He makes it work. Any road… In this era of roster churn Detroit Mercy is unusual in that not a single one of their players has scored a point for a team other than Detroit Mercy. I'll leave to you to decide what that means about the talent level of this group, but it at least speaks to the level of loyalty Mark Montgomery engenders. There's not a lot of data to mine here. This team scored 32 points against Marquette. They forced the three turnovers mentioned above, but none of them came from a steal. Tyler Spratt is currently the leading scorer. He scored eight against Marquette on 3-13 from the floor that he paired with four turnovers. Right behind him is Ayden Carter who was a glittering 3-11 from the floor but marred that performance with six turnovers and no assists. Carter also raked in six rebounds. Expect to see a lot of Xavier Istomin-Monroe, a 7-1 sophomore who played 29 minutes and had a stat line of 2/2/0 to go with his two blocks. Only one foul though, so there's that. Lance Stone and London Maiden round out the starting lineup. Stone is listed at 5-8, which means that if he's anything like most basketball players, he's actually about 5-6. Last season he was a decent three point shooter but shot a horrific 29.7% inside the arc, probably because he either couldn't see the rim or needs a big man to boost him. (If you read this, Lance, this is all in fun and I'm aware you would absolutely destroy me one on one despite me being a listed 5-10). London Maiden could be that boost giver. He's built like a guy who works physical labor, comes home for a good meal, then play wrestles with the kids until he falls asleep on the floor at 930. He was definitely watching that game if you try to change the channel. Maiden was an efficient scorer last season and will get on the offensive glass. – How does Xavier handle another poor opponent? There was a notable dip in the Musketeers execution and effort to begin last Friday against EMU. They looked like the prototypical team that knows they are going to win a game and just wants to get through it. They can do the same here, but a bit more verve from the off would be a good sign. – Is there an outside shooter here? Through two games, an admittedly small sample, X is shooting 31.1% behind the arc. Rolyns Aligbe (2-4) is the only player born in the US shooting it with any real success. Filip Borovicanin, Jovan Milicevic, and Gabriel Pozzato are a combined 8-17, the rest of the team excluding Aligbe is 4-25. That's not good. X doesn't need everyone to start pouring them in, but when three of the leaders are bigs and the other guy is a career 32% shooter, you might want an actual guard to start making a shot or two. – Who gets time? The minutes are incredibly even across the top 10 in rotation right now. Borovicanin leads at 24 per game, Pozzato is bringing up the rear at 15. At some point an actual rotation will have to begin to separate. That likely isn't against a team ranked below 300, but look for little clues. – Start quickly: Just put this thing to rest early and start to get to the point where X can practice what they need to do. There's no reason this should be a contest for longer than about ten minutes. – Teach Mike Nwoko not to foul: It's vaguely humorous right now to watch a 6-10 wall of muscle swat smaller players all over the place, it won't be come February and (God willing) late March. The odd thing about Nwoko is that his fouling tendency has gotten worse as he's developed. As a freshman at Miami (Fl) he played rotation minutes and never had more than three fouls. His rate was 4.2 per 40 minutes. That has slowly climbed to 6.4 so far this season. – Take care of the ball: Mercy "forced" three turnovers and didn't have a steal against Marquette. Xavier has, for reasons known mostly to themselves, been really wasterful with the ball so far this season. Now would be a good time to start to tighten it up. Iowa and Texas A&M are coming, and they will absolutely try to force mistakes.

title: AMD EPYC Venice-X CPUs Pack 1152 MB Of Cache Across 96 “Zen 6” Cores, With Boost Clocks Hitting 5.3 GHz In 2027 In The “Best 3D V-Cache CPU To Date” - Wccftech
content: AMD's EPYC 9006X or Venice-X CPUs will be launching in the second half of 2027, merging 3D V-Cache with a high-frequency Zen 6 core. According to AMD, EPYC 9006X "Venice-X" CPUs will be aimed at the Technical Compute and HPC segment. Their cache-rich design will make them a top choice for workloads that are memory-sensitive. Microsoft already spilled the beans on the AMD Venice-X chips, which will be deployed within its Azure HXv2 instances next year. The chips will feature up to 96 cores and 192 threads based on the classic Zen 6 core, with 2P platforms offering up to 192 "Zen 6" cores, 384 threads, over 5 GHz clock speeds (5.30 GHz max), and 50% more addressable cache per core as the 3D V-Cache stacks sit beneath the Zen 6 cores to offer increased technical compute and HPC capabilities. These chips will carry an impressive 1152 MB of L3 cache. Since there are eight V-Cache-boosted CCDs, each chip will house 96 MB of 3D V-Cache stacked over the Zen 6 CCD, which will pack 48 MB of L3 cache. That's 384 MB from the CCDs and 768 MB from the 3D V-Cache dies. Although AMD isn't changing the design methodology of its 3D V-Cache dies, which still leverage 3D Hybrid Bonding to achieve over 3x interconnect energy efficiency & over 15x the interconnect density compared to Micro Bump 3D, they are calling it the "Best 3D V-Cache Yet". Venice-X CPUs will support both DDR5-8000 & the industry's fastest MRDIMMs with up to 12,800 MT/s speeds across 16 channels on the SP7 platform. The platform will also carry up to 96 PCIe Gen6 lanes and offer up to 1638 GB/s of memory bandwidth per socket. Without sharing any specific numbers, AMD has confirmed that 3D V-Cache helps boost EDA workloads across major partners such as Siemens and Synopsys. Since the development of 3D V-Cache on EPYC CPUs, the company has seen massive deployments of 3D V-Cache and high-clock chips for EDA. The reason is that 3D V-Cache provides major benefits across EDA simulations, with improved per-core IPC, as seen in the following time chart: AMD's EPYC Venice-X CPUs are expected to roll out in 2H 2027 alongside the Verano "EPYC 9006 LP" lineup. AMD’s EPYC Venice-X processors are set to give technical compute and HPC a major boost when they arrive in the second half of 2027. By pairing high-frequency Zen 6 cores with a dramatically enlarged 3D V-Cache and the high-bandwidth SP7 platform, the chips should deliver strong gains for memory-sensitive workloads such as EDA simulations, while giving cloud providers like Microsoft a clear path to denser, higher-performance Azure instances. title: Lotus’s New V-8 Ferrari Fighter Is Coming in 2028; Here’s the Engine That Will Power It - Road & Track
content: Horse Powertrains has pulled the wraps off its first eight-cylinder powerplant, destined for the Lotus Type 135. Back in May, Lotus revealed its Focus 2030 strategy for the future, in which the storied British racing and sports car brand aims to return to its roots by “protecting what makes Lotus, Lotus.” What makes Lotus Lotus is, of course, at least partially combustion-powered performance cars that follow Colin Chapman’s maxim to “simplify and add lightness.” As a thrilling nod in that direction, Lotus confirmed plans to launch its first supercar, the Type 135—which may become the new Esprit. Now, we now know what will power it. On Tuesday, Horse Powertrain—a Geely subsidiary alongside Lotus—unveiled its new Horse W40 powerplant, which the company has confirmed the will power the Lotus Type 135. Horse also manufactures the new V-6 engine that will replace the supercharged Toyota V-6 in the Emira sports car. The Horse W40 is a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V8 with a hot-vee configuration, designed for use in high-performance hybrid vehicle platforms. It weighs just 441 pounds, but it can produce an impressive peak output of over 670 horsepower and 590 pound-feet of torque all on its own. When paired with a hybrid component, Lotus said the Type 135 will be able to deliver more than 986 hp. The Horse W40 uses a proprietary 8LDCT transmission. It’s an eight-speed transmission with a “sportscar-grade wet dual clutch.” Horse Powertrain claims a shift response time of less than 20 milliseconds, and the transmission can handle up to 774 pound-feet of torque. Lotus has not yet provided full details about the Type 135—those will be announced before the end of 2026—but the company has confirmed it plans to launch the new machine in 2028. The Type 135 will be all-new, distinct from the Emira; Lotus expects to build the supercar in Europe, unlike the China-made Eletre and Emeya EVs, which may reduce the potential exposure to American tariffs. Lotus has revealed a teaser image of the new car, showing a dual exhaust and a large diffuser. The Lotus Type 135 may not be the only application for this engine, either. Horse Powertrain says the engine’s low-end torque could be used for trucks and off-road vehicles, if you’ve been keeping a candle lit for Geely-owned Volvo to build a raucous but Scandinavian minimalist Mercedes G-Wagen competitor. title: The Honda CR-V Is Kicking Toyota RAV4 Butt, But It Won't Be That Way For Much Longer - CarBuzz
content: It's easy for an automaker to talk the talk, but Honda and the CR-V are definitely walking the walk this year, outperforming the industry-favorite Toyota RAV4 by a considerable margin. Unless Toyota suddenly decides to start dishing out half-off vouchers for new RAV4 models, it looks as if Honda has a clean run to the finish this year, and what's interesting is that Toyota handed Honda the win right from the very start this year. In 2016, Honda finished as the best-selling SUV in the US, with 357,335 units shifted across the entire year. That was 10 years ago, and it was also the last time Honda won that particular category. From 2017 through 2025, the RAV4 has been taking home the prize on Toyota's behalf instead. Last year, Toyota moved 479,288 units, while Honda trailed behind with 403,768 CR-Vs finding a new home. This year, however, the wind is back behind Honda's sails, and the data proves it. Honda's year-to-date (YTD) figures show that 371,659 CR-Vs have been sold, against 293,552 RAV4s – a difference of 78,107 units, as of the end of October. Roll the clock back 12 months, though, and the picture was entirely reversed. YTD figures for October 2025 showed 339,197 CR-Vs sold, against 397,797 RAV4s, a difference of 58,600 vehicles. So, what has Honda done in order to flip the script this year? As it happens, Honda didn't have to do much to take the sales lead. Instead, Toyota's situation caused the change. In short, the automaker released its all-new RAV4 this year. There was high demand, but unfortunately, Toyota was not able to keep up. Inventory shortages led to customers having to wait months and months for deliveries, and dealer stock was hanging around for a handful of days at most. Toyota prolonged production of the 2025 model, delaying the retooling of factories set to produce the 2026 model. As a result, production at Toyota's Kentucky and Ontario plants was far behind schedule. These factories have been churning out RAV4s at full capacity since Spring, but it has taken months for the company to catch up with the backlog. Buyers, faced with multiple month-long waits, naturally began looking at other options on the market, and Honda's CR-V was waiting patiently for them. However, 371,659 people aren't buying a Honda CR-V just because they don't want to wait for a RAV4 to show up. There are still plenty of reasons to pick a CR-V. Even when both SUVs are immediately available, some would still much rather jump into the Honda. For starters, Toyota made the bold decision to go hybrid-only with its latest RAV4 generation. Buyers still get the choice between a conventional or plug-in hybrid, but the gas-only option is gone. Over in Honda showrooms, however, customers will still find gas-only CR-Vs. Those who have traditionally steered away from hybrid cars, for whatever reason, might therefore find themselves trading in an old RAV4 at the Honda dealer rather than continuing behind the wheel of a Toyota. Now, buyers may want to steer clear of hybrids for various reasons. Those reasons might include wanting to avoid added mechanical complexity and extra weight, but the most obvious objection is the higher price tag that hybrid vehicles command. Admittedly, there isn't much difference between the base prices of the two SUV models under the microscope here. The CR-V kicks off at $31,520 in its base LX guise, while the base RAV4 LE has a $31,900 MSRP. A difference of just $380 is likely very easy to justify, especially when that extra premium buys a brand-new model with a far more efficient powertrain. However, in the real world, that price difference could actually be far greater. While RAV4 stock has been limited all year, and Toyota has been playing catch up, Honda has had plenty of CR-Vs to go around. The situation means that, as demand has outweighed supply, Toyota dealers have had no reason to offer incentives on RAV4s. In contrast, Honda has been in the advantageous position of being able to furnish buyers with little discounts here and there, in order to secure additional orders. The early months of 2026 saw Honda offering sub-$300 per month leases on a variety of both front- and all-wheel drive CR-Vs, while $1,000 purchase loyalty incentives were offered later in the year. Low-rate financing has been available, and up to $1,250 in cash incentives have also been available. Offers like these no doubt helped swing a few sales toward the CR-V when Toyota stock was running low. Nothing is promised, and certainly stranger things have happened, but smart money would bet on the Toyota RAV4 taking back its bestselling SUV crown next year. Ultimately, no matter how competitive the CR-V is, it's far longer in the tooth now, while Toyota's RAV4 is fresher, more powerful, more efficient, and not much more expensive. Plus, while stock levels haven't been there for much of 2026 to meet demand, that underlying demand has still been there, and with production now back up to speed, Toyota will be looking to take 2027 on with full force. And let's not forget that just last year Toyota demonstrated there was enough demand for almost 480,000 RAV4s to find a new home in the US. Are we potentially set to see the RAV4 reach its first half-million unit-years in 2027? Regardless of how next year plays out, the issues that have plagued the RAV4 throughout 2026 have enabled numerous other SUVs and crossovers to vie for the crown. Unless Toyota somehow manages to pull back from a near-80,000-unit deficit in the last two months of 2026, then that crown will ultimately rest upon the CR-V's head once again, interrupting the RAV4's near-decade-long reign. title: V Corps expands nightlife restrictions to permanently stationed soldiers in Europe - Stars and Stripes
content:
People enjoy their time at a bar on the weekend in Warsaw, Poland, on April 25, 2026. A new order signed by a V Corps leader prohibits U.S. soldiers permanently stationed in Poland from visiting bars, nightclubs and certain karaoke and hookah lounges. (Ebrahim Noroozi/AP) U.S. soldiers permanently stationed in Poland are now prohibited from visiting bars, nightclubs and certain karaoke and hookah lounges during off-duty hours. The tighter restrictions result from a revised V Corps general order that eliminates exemptions previously granted to troops stationed overseas. The Nov. 5 order from V Corps commander Lt. Gen. Thomas Feltey extends long-standing prohibitions for permanently assigned soldiers, including those living in off-installation housing in Poznan, Poland. “Our soldiers are in Europe for a purpose: to deter aggression and be ready to fight if called upon,” Feltey said in response to questions. A June 2024 version of the order specifically exempted soldiers serving on permanent change of station orders from most restrictions on off-limits establishments. That exemption is absent from the updated policy, which took effect immediately. Under the previous directive, restrictions on visiting bars, casinos, karaoke and hookah lounges and nightclubs did not apply to soldiers on PCS orders. V Corps soldiers at Camp Kosciuszko in Poznan were informed of the updated restrictions during a formation Friday, according to four soldiers who spoke with Stars and Stripes. One permanently assigned soldier who lives off base said the announcement caught personnel off guard and left them uncertain about how the new restrictions would affect their off-duty activities. “Everybody was kind of shocked and kind of trying to figure out what they can and can’t do,” said the soldier, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of fears about possible retaliation. The soldier, who previously served overseas and deployed, said the limitations make the permanent assignment feel more like a deployment than an opportunity to live abroad. The order applies to soldiers in V Corps’ designated area of responsibility, which covers 16 countries, including Poland, Romania and the Baltic states. The command estimates that more than 15,000 assigned, rotational and supporting personnel are subject to its provisions. Lt. Col. Vincent Gothard, V Corps director of public affairs, said the policy is a proactive measure intended to strengthen discipline and readiness along NATO’s eastern flank rather than a response to any particular incident or increase in misconduct. The order defines a prohibited bar as an establishment whose primary purpose is to serve alcohol and that does not provide tables and menus for seated dining. Karaoke and hookah lounges are prohibited when they primarily serve alcohol and lack seated dining accommodations. Nightclubs are defined as establishments with significant space dedicated to dancing, a disc jockey and a primary purpose of serving alcohol. Restaurants are not automatically prohibited simply because they serve alcohol or offer karaoke. However, the aforementioned soldier who spoke with Stars and Stripes said the definitions have created confusion about which businesses remain permissible, particularly establishments that serve food but transition into nightlife venues later in the evening. The soldier questioned whether troops would be required to leave an establishment when its kitchen closes, even if it had previously qualified as a restaurant. A V Corps noncommissioned officer permanently assigned to Camp Kosciuszko said no explanation was provided at the formation for why the restrictions had changed. The November order also changes several provisions governing alcohol consumption and overnight movement. Under the 2024 policy, soldiers on orders exceeding 30 days were prohibited from drinking alcohol during their first 96 hours in the U.S. European Command area of responsibility. That requirement does not appear in the updated order. The earlier policy also established a 0.15 blood alcohol concentration limit for permanently assigned soldiers. The November order specifically prohibits personnel on temporary change of station or temporary duty orders exceeding 30 days from drinking to the point of intoxication, defined as impairment or a blood alcohol concentration of 0.08. Both versions prohibit alcohol consumption within eight hours of duty or operating a vehicle. The updated order requires soldiers on temporary assignments exceeding 30 days to have an approved battle buddy when leaving an installation or forward operating site between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m., unless on approved leave or pass. The previous order established a battle-buddy requirement between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. for personnel subject to that provision. Permanently assigned soldiers are not required to have battle buddies for routine local travel, Gothard said. Other provisions address electronic cigarette purchases and use, alcohol possession at forward operating sites and a new prohibition against interfering with wild animals during official activities or while at forward operating sites, with limited exceptions. Violations of the order’s prohibited activity provisions are punishable under Article 92 of the Uniform Code of Military Justice and may result in disciplinary or adverse administrative action. Commanders are briefing soldiers and incorporating the updated requirements into in-processing procedures, Gothard said. ShaTyra Cox is a reporter for Stars and Stripes based in Poznan, Poland. She has worked in military communities in the U.S. and abroad since 2013. title: Mums v Big Pharma review – the ‘bored, hysterical housewives’ who exposed a horrifying scandal - The Guardian
content: Janet Williams and Emma Murphy both had children with disabilities, then started doing some digging … and uncovered a jaw-dropping medical fiasco that rivals thalidomide. Long may they fight! Tales of corporate or governmental wrongdoing are often hugely complicated. Documents destroyed, witnesses untraceable, endless obfuscations and legal intricacies invoked. If the people doing the uncovering are ordinary folk, unarmed with fancy lawyers or untrained in the ways of big business or statecraft, the story often becomes even more of a switchback ride before the mind-boggling whole is laid bare. Just occasionally, however, the story is very simple (though no less mind-boggling). Such a case is that of the sodium valproate scandal, uncovered thanks to a campaign that was started 17 years ago by two mothers who began to suspect that their children’s disabilities had a specific cause. Janet Williams had two sons with developmental delays. For years she was told by doctors that there was nothing wrong: “You truly believed that if there was something wrong or something that needed explanation, they would tell you,” she says now, remembering her naive younger self and her trust in the medical profession. Then, in 2009, the boys were referred to a specialist who almost casually informed her that their condition was probably a result of her epilepsy medication, Epilim. It was the brand name for sodium valproate, discovered in 1962 to be an effective anti-seizure drug, and also used to treat bipolar disorder. By the time Williams was having her children in the 1990s, it was one of the most widely prescribed treatments for epilepsy in the UK. Williams started distributing leaflets in her home town of Pilling, Lancashire, telling her story and asking other potentially afflicted families to get in touch. They did. They had questions she couldn’t answer, so she started researching everything she could at Manchester Central library. Then she made the news and Emma Murphy from nearby Bury, five of whose children (out of six) had similar difficulties to Williams’s after exposure to Epilim, got in touch. To Murphy’s continuing amusement – “I’d just been reading women’s magazines and sitting at home watching Coronation Street!” – they began putting together evidence that would eventually reveal a scandal to rival thalidomide in scale and suffering. Alongside the mothers’ story runs that of Prof Jill Clayton-Smith, a clinical geneticist working in Manchester in the mid-90s, who began to notice a recurring cluster of features among the children born to women treated for epilepsy. She investigated further and presented her findings – including a 1984 US paper describing “foetal valproate syndrome” – at a conference. “It wasn’t received as well as I’d hoped,” she says delicately. The male-dominated audience essentially scoffed at her “anecdotal” data and ignored it. Prof David Chadwick, however, encouraged her to embark on a formal study that could not be refuted. Williams’s children would become part of it and it would eventually help determine that sodium valproate carries a 10% risk of causing physical malformations and a 30-40% risk of causing serious neurodevelopmental disorders in those exposed. The drug is estimated to have affected 39,399 babies since the risk was first identified. In 2011, Murphy, Williams and 138 other families were undertaking a class action suit against the drug manufacturer Sanofi Aventis. Excitement and hope were building when suddenly their legal aid was withdrawn after they were deemed unlikely to succeed, and lawyers formally discontinued action. By 2013 they had regrouped and began investigating the apparent regulatory failure in licensing the drug for use by women of childbearing age. They had several futile meetings in Westminster. “We were referred to as ‘bored, hysterical housewives’,” says Murphy. Williams remembers an official turning to her to ask if she understood what a word meant. She did. “The way they dealt with us was sickening … But it drove me on.” They started secretly recording the meetings. We hear audio of someone saying: “The neurologists weren’t in favour of having this acknowledgment of risk … Doctors don’t like being told what to do,” and suggesting that patient warnings on packaging weren’t necessary because people could find the information on the internet if they wanted – “Your Facebook site’s great!” “The ignorance,” says Williams. “The arrogance.” “Bastards,” murmurs Murphy. The thalidomide campaign team advised them to go to the National Archives at Kew and look for the meeting notes from the Committee on Safety of Medicines (CSM) when the drug came on the market. In 2015 they found the smoking gun: the CSM’s response to Sanofi’s statement to them that the drug was harmful to foetuses. To warn about this, it said, would cause women “fruitless anxiety.” So nobody was told anything. This is where medical misogyny, a cancer in the system that corrupts everything it touches, inexorably leads. There was a government review, there was handwringing, there was the promise two years ago of state compensation. There have been no payments yet to the estimated 20,000 families affected by the drug. But bored, hysterical housewives never give up. God bless them, and damn the rest. Mums v Big Pharma aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer
